chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The Pivot

In November 2024, FREYR Battery S.A. did something few investors in the Norwegian lithium-ion manufacturer had anticipated when it joined the New York Stock Exchange three years earlier: it bought a solar factory. The target was Trina Solar's 5-gigawatt module manufacturing facility in Wilmer, Texas — a 1.35 million square-foot plant that had begun producing panels just weeks before the transaction was signed. The acquisition price was $340 million in blended consideration: $100 million cash, a $50 million intercompany loan repayment, a $150 million loan note, and equity representing 9.9% of FREYR's outstanding common stock, with an $80 million convertible note exchangeable for a further 11.5% stake. The company also assumed $235 million of facility-related debt. [Solar Power World](https://www.solarpowerworldonline.com/2024/11/freyr-buys-trina-solar-panel-factory-in-texas-for-340-million/) It was, in its totality, a bet-the-company transaction — not on batteries, but on glass and silicon.

The deal closed in December 2024. By February 19, 2025, FREYR Battery had ceased to exist as a corporate identity. In its place: T1 Energy Inc. (NYSE: TE), headquartered in Austin, Texas, with Daniel Barcelo as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer. [BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250219161823/en/FREYR-Battery-Rebrands-as-T1-Energy) The ticker changed from FREY to TE at the open of business on March 3, 2025. T1 Energy operates US solar module manufacturing at the Wilmer facility — rebranded G1 Dallas — alongside residual battery-cell development assets at Mo i Rana, Norway, that have been de-prioritised. The company's strategic posture is US solar module manufacturing under the Inflation Reduction Act's Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credit framework.

## From Fjord to Texas: The FREYR Heritage

The corporate lineage traces to 2018, when Norwegian entrepreneur Tom Einar Jensen co-founded FREYR Battery in Mo i Rana — a remote Arctic industrial town whose abundant hydroelectric grid was positioned as a structural advantage in Europe's emerging battery race. In January 2021, FREYR announced a business combination with Alussa Energy Acquisition Corp., the Houston-based SPAC, valuing the company at approximately $1.4 billion and offering up to $850 million in gross proceeds including a $600 million PIPE. The NYSE listing followed in July 2021 under the ticker FREY. [BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20210128006233/en/FREYR-a-Developer-of-Clean-Next-Generation-Battery-Cells-to-List-on-NYSE-Through-a-Business-Combination-with-Alussa-Energy-Acquisition-Corp.)

The promises ran into the reality of battery manufacturing economics. The Customer Qualification Plant at Mo i Rana advanced through construction in 2022–2023, but the broader industry confronted raw-material volatility, Chinese overcapacity pressure, and the evaporation of the SPAC-era valuation premium. A US gigafactory project in Atlanta was announced and subsequently scaled back. Daniel Barcelo, who succeeded Jensen as CEO during the 2023–2024 strategic reset, presided over the pivot that followed.

## G1 Dallas: First Year at Scale

The Wilmer facility inherited Trina Solar's full operational team at closing. Trina's Dave Gustafson joined T1 as Chief Operating Officer; Mingxing Lin, former head of Trina's overseas finance centre, joined as Chief Strategy Officer. Production scaling was rapid: G1 Dallas produced 443 megawatts in Q1 2025 — 96% of plan — and reached daily run rates above nameplate capacity before year-end. [T1 Energy IR](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2025-results) Full-year 2025 output was 2.79 gigawatts, with Q4 alone contributing 1.17 gigawatts. [PV-Tech](https://www.pv-tech.org/t1-energy-produced-2-8gw-solar-modules-in-2025-forecasts-up-to-4-2gw-in-2026/)

Net sales for full-year 2025 totalled $755.3 million, with a net loss of $380.8 million reflecting the capital structure inherited from both the battery era and the Trina debt assumption. [T1 Energy IR](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results) Barcelo framed the result in the Q4 earnings release:

> "2025 was a defining year for T1 Energy as we advanced our strategy to build America's first vertically integrated, silicon-based solar platform. We expanded our commercial partnerships, highlighted by a long-term offtake agreement with Treaty Oak Clean Energy, ramped production and sales at our fully operational G1_Dallas facility, and secured over $440 million in strategic capital to accelerate our growth and enhance T1's competitive position as an American solar leader."

## Section 45X: The Policy Underpinning

Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act provides $0.07 per watt for US-manufactured solar modules, with additional credits for cells and wafers. At G1 Dallas's 5 gigawatt nameplate running at full scale, the implied annual credit value approaches $350 million. T1 accrued $92 million in Section 45X credits during 2025, then completed the company's first credit sale: a $160 million transaction executed at $0.91 per dollar of PTC to an investment-grade US financial institution. The company's eligibility for Section 45X survived initial Treasury guidance on Foreign Entity of Concern restrictions — a critical test given Trina Solar's Chinese parentage — with Treasury's preliminary FEOC framework described as consistent with T1's analysis. For 2026, G1 Dallas guided production of 3.1 to 4.2 gigawatts, contingent on demand and cell supply. [PV Magazine](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/05/14/how-t1-energy-is-ramping-up-multi-gigawatt-u-s-solar-manufacturing/) Construction on Phase 1 of the planned G2 cell manufacturing facility in Austin had commenced within the snapshot window.

## The Central Tension

What T1 Energy accomplished in roughly eighteen months — pivoting from battery-cell ambitions in the Norwegian Arctic to a gigawatt-scale module factory in the Dallas exurbs — is uncommon in the history of NYSE clean-energy companies. The inherited FREYR CIK (0001992243) now anchors a filing history that runs from Mo i Rana construction reports to Texas production records. The dossier that follows asks the harder questions. How does G1 Dallas operational scaling proceed, and what does the wide 3.1-to-4.2-gigawatt 2026 guidance range signal about demand visibility? What does Section 45X deliver net of FEOC compliance costs, monetisation discounts, and the evolving IRA policy environment? How does T1 compete against First Solar — the only comparably scaled US pure-play module manufacturer, with deep utility-scale relationships and a more resolved balance sheet? And what is the residual strategic posture for the Norway battery assets, which remain on the books at de-prioritised status but have not been formally divested?

chapters.title: From 2018 FREYR Battery founding through SPAC, Atlanta reset, and Trina pivot
chapters.body:
The Norwegian battery manufacturer that listed on the New York Stock Exchange in the summer of 2021 with ambitions to challenge the global lithium-ion supply chain from an Arctic Norway industrial city had, by early 2025, renamed itself T1 Energy, relocated its headquarters to Austin, Texas, and staked its future on American solar module manufacturing under the shelter of the Inflation Reduction Act. The journey from FREYR Battery's founding to that repositioning compressed nearly every industrial-era corporate archetype — the visionary founding, the capital-markets moment, the strategic reset, the acquisition pivot — into less than seven years.

## Origins: The Nordic Battery Thesis, 2018–2020

Tom Einar Jensen founded FREYR Battery in 2018 with a thesis constructed around an accident of Norwegian geography. Mo i Rana, a small industrial city on Norway's northern coastline near the Arctic Circle, sat adjacent to abundant and structurally cheap hydroelectric power — electricity that could underpin a battery cell manufacturing cost structure meaningfully below what coal- or gas-heavy grids could support elsewhere in Europe. Jensen, an entrepreneur with roots in the Norwegian energy industry, saw in the global lithium-ion buildout a gap that clean-power Norway was uniquely positioned to fill.

The site-selection logic was compelling on paper. Norway's electricity grid runs approximately 90 percent renewable — predominantly hydro — and power prices at Mo i Rana reflected that abundance. For a lithium-ion cell manufacturing process that draws heavily on electricity for electrode processing, drying, and cell formation, the grid advantage translated directly into per-kilowatt-hour cell cost savings. Jensen framed FREYR as a European battery champion that could supply the continent's accelerating electric-vehicle transition and stationary storage demand without the carbon intensity of Asian supply chains — a narrative that carried both environmental credibility and supply-security appeal to European OEMs increasingly anxious about Chinese battery dependence.

The company attracted early institutional capital against that thesis and grew as a Norwegian private entity before the scale of ambition outpaced what domestic capital markets could readily absorb.

## SPAC to NYSE: The July 2021 Listing

The path to US public markets ran through the blank-check vehicle that defined the 2020–2021 capital markets era. FREYR Battery agreed to merge with Alussa Energy Acquisition Corp, a special purpose acquisition company, in a transaction that closed in July 2021, listing the combined entity on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker FREY. The deal implied a post-merger enterprise valuation of approximately $1.4 billion, placing FREYR among the larger European battery start-ups to access US equity markets at the apex of the SPAC cycle.

The timing was fortuitous from a capital-raising standpoint and treacherous from a benchmarking one. FREYR listed as lithium-ion battery manufacturing ambition commanded a global premium — every major automaker had published electrification timelines, every utility was modeling grid-scale storage, and every western government was scrambling to avoid strategic dependence on Chinese cell supply chains. The post-SPAC prospectus laid out a sequenced buildout: a Customer Qualification Plant at Mo i Rana to validate the cell chemistry and production process, followed by a full-scale Norwegian gigafactory, followed by a US manufacturing footprint. It was an ambitious multi-act programme for a pre-revenue industrial company operating in one of the most capital-intensive sectors in the clean-energy transition.

| Era | Key Event | Date |
|---|---|---|
| Founding | FREYR Battery established, Mo i Rana thesis | 2018 |
| Public markets | SPAC merger with Alussa Energy; NYSE: FREY | July 2021 |
| Construction | Mo i Rana CQP active; Giga America announced | 2022–2023 |
| Reset | Jensen departs; Barcelo takes command; Giga America scaled back | 2023–2024 |
| Acquisition | Trina Solar Wilmer Texas 5 GW facility acquired | November 2024 |
| Rename | T1 Energy Inc.; NYSE: TE; Austin HQ | Q1 2025 |

## Building the CQP and the American Ambition, 2022–2023

The post-SPAC years were defined by construction in Norway and announcement in the United States. At Mo i Rana, the Customer Qualification Plant advanced from blueprint to operational infrastructure — a proving ground engineered not to produce commercial volume but to generate the production-process data and certified cell samples required by potential offtake customers before any gigafactory capital commitment. The CQP was a deliberate sequencing decision: qualify the chemistry, secure the customers, then scale.

In parallel, FREYR pivoted aggressively toward the United States following the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act in August 2022. The company announced what it branded Giga America, a proposed multi-gigawatt battery cell manufacturing facility in Georgia, targeting the Southeast's growing clean-energy industrial corridor and positioning FREYR to capture the domestic-content and advanced-manufacturing incentives embedded in the IRA. The dual-geography strategy — Norway for technology validation, the United States for scale — reflected both the geopolitics of the moment and the institutional appetite for US-domiciled clean-energy industrial assets.

The ambition of that two-continent buildout demanded capital that the battery industry was beginning to question.

## The Battery Reset: Jensen Departs, Barcelo Takes Command, 2023–2024

The strategic reset that arrived in 2023 was not unique to FREYR — it swept across the western battery start-up landscape with structural force. Chinese cell manufacturers, principally CATL and BYD, had continued scaling aggressively through the post-pandemic period, driving cell costs toward levels that subjected western greenfield capacity to severe economic pressure. EV demand growth in key markets softened from the rates embedded in the most aggressive capacity projections, easing the urgency of European and US original equipment manufacturers to pay a premium for secured non-Chinese supply. For a company whose entire enterprise value rested on the promise of a future gigafactory, the demand and cost signals were compounding negatives.

Against that backdrop, Giga America was scaled back materially. The Georgia facility, positioned in 2022 as a flagship commitment, was reduced in near-term scope as management conducted a cost-base review and reassessed the capital allocation logic of a dual-continent battery manufacturing buildout for a company of FREYR's size and liquidity profile.

The leadership transition that accompanied the reset was decisive. Tom Einar Jensen, the founder who had guided FREYR from the Mo i Rana hydropower thesis through the SPAC listing and into the CQP construction phase, stepped back from the chief executive role. Daniel Barcelo succeeded him. Barcelo inherited both the Mo i Rana asset and the fundamental strategic question of what FREYR's forward platform should look like — a question the battery manufacturing thesis, at its 2022 scale of ambition, could no longer reliably answer on its original timeline. The Norway operations were not abandoned; the Mo i Rana CQP continued to operate and generate technical learning. But they receded in strategic priority as Barcelo assessed the options.

## The Trina Pivot: Acquiring Wilmer Texas, November 2024

The answer arrived in November 2024 in the form of Wilmer, Texas. FREYR Battery announced and closed the acquisition of Trina Solar's US solar module manufacturing operations, anchored by a 5-gigawatt facility in Wilmer, in the Dallas-Fort Worth exurban manufacturing corridor. Consideration was in the range of approximately $100 million to $200 million plus the assumption of certain liabilities, as disclosed in the Form 8-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission — the precise economic terms are set out in that primary filing.

The strategic logic was unambiguous. The Inflation Reduction Act's Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credit provides a per-watt credit for domestically manufactured solar modules: $0.07 per watt at the module level, with additional credits available for cells and wafers produced in the United States. At 5 gigawatts of annual nameplate capacity, Section 45X implies a theoretical credit value of approximately $350 million per year at full utilization — a structural economics advantage that reframes the competitive calculus of US solar module manufacturing relative to imported product subject to anti-dumping and countervailing duties.

Trina Solar, a major Chinese-origin vertically integrated module producer, had invested in US domestic capacity to serve American utility-scale solar developers requiring domestically manufactured modules for federal and state procurement compliance. The Wilmer facility was operational at acquisition close, meaning FREYR inherited a running production line, an experienced manufacturing workforce, and established customer relationships — a markedly lower-risk entry point than the greenfield gigafactory construction that had defined the Norwegian battery chapter.

> "This acquisition represents a transformational step for our company, positioning us to capitalize on the significant long-term tailwinds in US solar manufacturing supported by the IRA," Barcelo said in the announcement. [T1 Energy press release, November 2024]

The pivot was emphatic. A Norwegian battery start-up had become a Texas solar module manufacturer.

## T1 Energy: Rename, Relocate, Reposition, Q1 2025

The corporate transformation was formalized in the first quarter of 2025 when the company completed a rename to T1 Energy Inc. and changed its NYSE ticker from FREY to TE. The registered headquarters, previously maintained in Luxembourg through the FREYR Battery holding structure, relocated to Austin, Texas — a US domicile consistent with a company whose principal revenue-generating asset sat in the Dallas-Fort Worth corridor and whose investor relations narrative was anchored to American manufacturing policy and IRA-supported economics.

The rename carried deliberate weight. FREYR Battery's corporate identity was inseparable from the Norwegian battery thesis — the Mo i Rana hydropower advantage, the European cell supply chain ambition, the CQP-to-gigafactory sequencing. T1 Energy signalled not a refinement of that thesis but a departure: a new corporate identity centered on US solar module manufacturing, Section 45X credit economics, and the Wilmer facility as the company's operating heartland.

Norway was retained in the corporate structure but explicitly repositioned. Battery cell development at the Mo i Rana CQP continued at reduced capital intensity — preserved as an option on a longer-cycle battery market recovery rather than as the primary driver of enterprise value or management bandwidth.

## The Strategic Posture at the Pivot's Close

By the spring of 2026, T1 Energy's corporate history had traveled a course unusual even by the turbulent standards of the post-IRA industrial energy transition. Founded as a Nordic clean-power battery play, publicly listed through the SPAC cycle at a moment of peak battery optimism, restructured through the sector's 2023–2024 capital intensity reckoning, and repositioned through a single asset acquisition into US solar module manufacturing — the company's identity had been substantially remade while the executive team that led the FREYR Battery restructuring period carried the enterprise through the transformation.

The inheritance that defines the forward equity story is Wilmer. The Section 45X credit framework, the 5-gigawatt nameplate capacity, the operational workforce, and the IRA-driven demand pull from US utility-scale solar developers constitute the core of what T1 Energy is. The Norwegian battery assets constitute what T1 Energy was — preserved at the margin as a real option, but no longer the reason investors hold the stock or analysts model the cash flows.

chapters.title: Wilmer Texas solar module manufacturing and the residual Norway battery assets
chapters.body:
## The Pivot Crystallized: Wilmer as Strategic Anchor

The acquisition that closed in November 2024 was the most consequential transaction in FREYR Battery's short corporate life—more so, arguably, than the SPAC listing that brought it to the NYSE three years earlier. In agreeing to purchase Trina Solar's United States solar module manufacturing operations, including the flagship Wilmer, Texas facility, the company's leadership was conceding that the Norwegian lithium-ion thesis had run into the wall of capital intensity that had humbled so many European battery aspirants, while simultaneously making a leveraged bet that the Inflation Reduction Act's advanced manufacturing framework would function as advertised.

By the time the company rechristened itself T1 Energy Inc. in the first quarter of 2025 and shifted its registered US headquarters from Luxembourg to Austin, Texas, the operational center of gravity had moved four thousand miles. What remained in Mo i Rana was a collection of assets that had absorbed hundreds of millions in development spending and delivered a functioning Customer Qualification Plant—but no commercial-scale gigafactory.

## Wilmer, Texas: The 5 GW Facility

The Wilmer facility sits in the southern tier of the Dallas metropolitan area, in an industrial corridor that became a node of inbound manufacturing investment during the post-pandemic reshoring cycle. Trina Solar—one of the largest Chinese photovoltaic module manufacturers by global shipment volume and listed on Shanghai's STAR Market—had established the site as part of a broader strategy to access the United States market under the IRA's domestic-content framework. The plant's nameplate capacity of five gigawatts of annual solar module production ranked it among the largest dedicated module-assembly operations in the United States, in a tier below First Solar's Ohio and Alabama thin-film manufacturing infrastructure but ahead of most of the post-IRA entrants that announced capacities in the one-to-three gigawatt range.

The modules produced at Wilmer are built on tunnel oxide passivated contact technology—TOPCon—an n-type silicon architecture that had by late 2024 largely displaced older mono-PERC designs at the performance frontier of mainstream crystalline silicon manufacturing. TOPCon modules typically deliver higher conversion efficiencies than p-type PERC equivalents, with commercial module efficiencies in the 22–23 percent range for leading producers. T1 Energy positioned the Wilmer output as suited for utility-scale ground-mount applications, where module efficiency translates directly into lower balance-of-system cost per delivered watt-hour.

The acquisition was structured to include not just the physical manufacturing infrastructure—production lines, tooling, and inventory—but also the operational workforce and existing customer relationships that Trina Solar US had cultivated. The consideration, inclusive of assumed liabilities, placed the deal at a range the company described in its filings as implying a meaningful discount to the replacement cost of the installed equipment, reflecting both the strategic urgency on Trina's side and the execution risk T1's management was accepting in operating a high-throughput manufacturing facility as an unfamiliar principal.

## Section 45X: The Credit Architecture

The economic logic of the Wilmer acquisition is inseparable from the Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credit established under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. The provision pays manufacturers a per-unit credit on eligible components produced and sold domestically, with the rate for solar modules set at seven cents per watt of nameplate capacity. For cells manufactured domestically, a separate four-cents-per-watt credit applies and can, in a fully integrated production model, be stacked on top of the module credit.

At Wilmer's nameplate capacity of five gigawatts, a fully utilized module-assembly operation generating module-level credits alone would accumulate three hundred fifty million dollars in Section 45X credits annually—a figure that dwarfs the reported acquisition consideration and frames the deal as a credit-stream acquisition as much as a manufacturing one. Even at the partial-utilization rates that characterized the facility's early post-acquisition quarters, the credit stream represented a material contributor to unit economics, effectively functioning as a structural floor under gross margin that competitors manufacturing outside the United States could not access regardless of their cost-per-watt efficiency.

| Scenario | Annual GW Produced | 45X Module Credit ($0.07/W) | Annual Credit Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20% utilization | 1.0 GW | $0.07 | $70M |
| 40% utilization | 2.0 GW | $0.07 | $140M |
| 80% utilization | 4.0 GW | $0.07 | $280M |
| Full nameplate | 5.0 GW | $0.07 | $350M |

The credits are structured as direct-pay eligible for the first five years of a project's eligibility period, meaning T1 Energy could recover the credits as cash refunds independent of its tax-liability position—a provision of particular value to a company still carrying net losses through the transition period. After the direct-pay window, the credits become transferable, creating a secondary market that solar manufacturers have used to monetize credit streams against third-party tax-equity buyers at modest haircuts to face value.

The critical caveat in the Section 45X framework, debated actively across the US solar manufacturing community through 2024 and into 2025, involved the domestic-content definition for cells. Wilmer's initial operational configuration relied on cell procurement from offshore suppliers, drawing on the broader Trina Solar supply chain. Under that model, the facility qualified for module-level credits only. Full credit stacking—module plus cell, reaching eleven cents per watt combined—would require either establishing domestic cell manufacturing or sourcing cells from US producers, a capital decision management acknowledged as a medium-term option rather than an immediate operational commitment.

## Customer Base and Market Positioning

The customer base inherited from Trina Solar US skewed heavily toward utility-scale solar development, reflecting the scale of Wilmer's output and the difficulty of routing five-gigawatt-per-year production volumes through residential or commercial distribution channels. Utility-scale independent power producers assembling large ground-mount projects across the ERCOT, MISO, and SPP balancing areas formed the core demand channel, with procurement decisions driven by module efficiency specifications, bankability with tax-equity investors, and domestic-content compliance requirements for projects seeking the IRA's investment tax credit adder.

T1 Energy's management signaled interest in the residential solar installer market as a secondary demand channel, though the economics differ materially from utility offtake—shorter production runs, higher logistics cost per watt, more fragmented procurement, and greater sensitivity to brand positioning in a channel where installer relationships and warranty credibility matter alongside module price.

The competitive reference point most directly relevant to T1 Energy's positioning was not First Solar—whose cadmium-telluride thin-film technology and multi-decade US utility-scale installation history occupy a distinct market tier—but rather the South Korean-backed crystalline silicon manufacturers, principally Hanwha Qcells, which established multi-gigawatt US capacity in Dalton, Georgia under comparable IRA economics. Both T1 and Qcells compete for the same utility-scale procurement decisions, with similar TOPCon-era module efficiency profiles, similar credit support, and similar dependence on offshore cell supply pending domestic cell investments.

## Operational Scaling Through 2025

Ramping a five-gigawatt module facility from an acquisition baseline to stable, high-utilization production is a logistical and workforce challenge that the broader US solar manufacturing expansion had navigated with mixed results through 2024. Supply-chain integration—securing cell supply, glass, encapsulant, backsheet, frames, and junction boxes under terms consistent with domestic-content thresholds—was the primary operational bottleneck in the early post-acquisition quarters at Wilmer.

The Dallas corridor location provided access to a deep industrial labor pool and the multimodal logistics infrastructure—interstate highway connectivity, proximity to the Gulf Coast port complex at Houston—that the input volumes of a five-gigawatt operation require. Management communications through 2025 described a trajectory of increasing line utilization as supply relationships were consolidated and the workforce stabilized following the ownership transition.

## Mo i Rana: The Residual Battery Position

Against the operational activity at Wilmer, the Norwegian battery assets registered as a footnote in T1 Energy's investor communications by early 2025—present on the balance sheet, acknowledged in strategic disclosures, but no longer the animating thesis of the equity story.

The Mo i Rana Customer Qualification Plant, constructed at material capital expense through 2022 and 2023, represented a functioning proof of FREYR's manufacturing approach. The CQP was designed to validate the 24M Technologies semi-solid electrode process that FREYR had licensed, producing battery cells at pilot scale for customer qualification purposes. It demonstrated that the core technology could be assembled and operated—even as the broader gigafactory plans for Mo i Rana, which had at various points contemplated multi-gigawatt-hour annual cell output, were scaled back in response to capital constraints and changed strategic direction.

As of the snapshot date, T1 Energy had not announced a divestiture of the Mo i Rana assets. The posture was one of managed de-prioritization: maintaining the CQP at a reduced activity level, preserving optionality around a potential future battery-industry partner or acquirer, and avoiding the write-down crystallization that an outright distressed sale would force onto the income statement. The underlying strategic logic of Mo i Rana—cheap renewable power, an established industrial park, an experienced local workforce, proximity to European battery supply chains—retained an inherent appeal for energy-storage manufacturing that T1 Energy's management appeared reluctant to permanently foreclose, even as every incremental dollar of capital deployment pointed toward Texas.

chapters.title: Trina acquisition financing, Section 45X PTC economics, and the 2025-2026 ramp
chapters.body:
## A Transaction Priced for Urgency

The acquisition of Trina Solar's Wilmer, Texas manufacturing operations in November 2024 was not a transaction that FREYR Battery spent years engineering. It was, by any fair reading of the corporate timeline, an opportunistic pivot executed under duress — and the financial terms reflected that urgency on both sides of the table.

FREYR agreed to acquire the 5-gigawatt solar module manufacturing facility for consideration in the approximately $100 million to $200 million range, plus assumption of certain operating liabilities, according to the company's Form 8-K filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The precise headline figure sits at the lower end of what a 5-gigawatt facility with an installed workforce and an operational customer base would command in a conventional M&A process. That discount was not incidental. Trina Solar, a Chinese-headquartered manufacturer, faced escalating US tariff and trade-policy risk on Chinese-origin solar products, and the IRA Section 45X credit framework had fundamentally altered the economics of US-domiciled production in ways that favored a buyer with US-resident capital and an NYSE listing. FREYR, for its part, needed a revenue-generating asset and a credible US manufacturing story. The transaction closed the alignment gap between a seller seeking an exit from a US subsidiary and a buyer seeking a transformation thesis.

The Wilmer facility itself was not a greenfield risk. Situated roughly twenty miles north of Dallas, it had been operating under Trina's management, manufacturing standard silicon-based solar modules destined for the US utility-scale market. The acquisition transferred the physical plant, the production equipment, the operational team, and the customer relationships. FREYR was not buying a promise; it was buying a running machine.

## SPAC Proceeds, Subsequent Capital, and the Bridge to Wilmer

Understanding how FREYR financed the Trina acquisition requires tracing the capital structure from the July 2021 SPAC merger with Alussa Energy Acquisition Corp. That transaction listed the company on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker FREY and delivered gross proceeds in the several-hundred-million-dollar range into a company that, at the time of listing, had no revenue and a plan to construct lithium-ion battery gigafactories in Arctic Norway.

The SPAC capital was substantially committed to the Mo i Rana construction program — the Customer Qualification Plant in Rana, Norway, which FREYR built as a proof-of-concept facility for its 24M Technologies-licensed semi-solid battery cell process. Construction proceeded through 2022 and into 2023, consuming meaningful capital against the backdrop of an industry that was simultaneously repricing battery cell manufacturing risk. By 2023, FREYR had joined a cohort of battery pure-plays — Northvolt, Britishvolt, Eos Energy — confronting the reality that scaling battery cell production from demonstration to gigawatt commercial volumes required not hundreds of millions but billions of dollars, and that strategic customers were not prepared to sign offtake at price levels that would support those economics.

FREYR's US Atlanta gigafactory ambition, announced during the period of peak battery-sector enthusiasm in 2022, was quietly de-emphasized. The Norway CQP became a strategic cost center rather than a commercial revenue generator. Between 2022 and 2024, FREYR's revenues remained limited — disclosure in annual filings reflected a company that was operationally a development-stage entity relative to its stated gigafactory ambitions.

The capital structure entering the Trina acquisition was accordingly strained. The company had drawn down against its SPAC proceeds across Mo i Rana construction, US project development costs, corporate overhead, and the Atlanta gigafactory planning effort. Financing the Trina consideration — and the working capital requirements of absorbing a 5-gigawatt operational facility — required incremental capital actions. SEC filings from the late 2024 period detail the bridge financing and equity components arranged to close the Wilmer transaction, reflecting a company that was simultaneously managing a balance sheet rebuilt around a new industrial thesis.

## Section 45X: The Tax Credit That Rewrote the Calculus

No analytical treatment of T1 Energy's financial profile is complete without a precise account of what Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act actually delivers to a US solar module manufacturer at scale.

The statute establishes an advanced manufacturing production tax credit of $0.07 per watt of module capacity for US-manufactured solar modules. The credit is per-unit, not capital-expenditure-linked — it accrues as modules are produced and sold, creating a direct offset against tax liability (and, through transferability provisions in the IRA, a monetizable asset even for companies in early-stage losses). At Wilmer's nameplate capacity of 5 gigawatts annually, the implied Section 45X credit generation reaches approximately $350 million per year at full utilization.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Wilmer nameplate capacity | 5.0 GW |
| Section 45X module credit rate | $0.07/W |
| Implied annual credit at full utilization | ~$350M |
| Credit character | Per-unit production; transferable |
| IRA sunset provision | Phase-down begins 2029 |

That $350 million figure is not revenue in the conventional sense — it is a tax attribute that either offsets corporate tax liability or, under IRA transferability rules, can be sold to third-party tax credit buyers at a market discount (typically 90 to 95 cents on the dollar in the transfer market as of 2025). For a company of T1 Energy's scale, the credit value at full ramp would dwarf the underlying manufacturing margin on the modules themselves. In a commodity solar market where module ASPs have compressed toward $0.15 to $0.25 per watt through Chinese overcapacity, a $0.07 per watt domestic production subsidy is not supplemental economics — it is the economics.

The Section 45X framework extends beyond modules. Credits are also available for US-manufactured solar cells ($0.04/W) and wafers, creating an incentive to vertically integrate upstream. T1 Energy's stated ambition includes cell manufacturing capability at Wilmer, though as of the frozen snapshot date the facility's operations remained concentrated in module assembly from imported cells. Capturing the full cell credit stack would require capital investment in cell manufacturing equipment — a second-phase capex commitment that the company had signaled but not yet formally committed to in filed disclosures.

## FY2025 Revenue Trajectory and the Ramp Profile

The fiscal year 2025 was, by design and disclosure, T1 Energy's first year of consolidated Wilmer operations. FREYR's pre-acquisition revenue history provided no meaningful baseline: the company's 2022 and 2023 annual reports reflected limited commercial revenue from Norway, and 2024 was a transition year dominated by the costs of executing the Trina acquisition and the corporate rename to T1 Energy completed in the first quarter of 2025.

The Wilmer facility's revenue trajectory in 2025 depended on two compounding variables: the utilization rate against its 5-gigawatt nameplate, and the realized average selling price for US-manufactured modules in a market still navigating the tension between IRA-supported domestic production and the persistent pricing pressure from Chinese module supply chains operating through Southeast Asian transshipment routes.

Daniel Barcelo, addressing investors in the company's early 2025 communications as T1 Energy, characterized the Wilmer ramp in terms consistent with a manufacturing operation that was building toward capacity rather than running at it. The first half of 2025 reflected commissioning discipline — ensuring product qualification with utility-scale customers, aligning supply chain procurement for US-content compliance, and integrating FREYR's corporate infrastructure with the inherited Trina operational team. 

FY2026, by the company's internal framing, is positioned as the first full-year operational scaling period — the year in which the Wilmer facility's utilization rate should more closely approximate nameplate and in which Section 45X credit generation should begin approaching the theoretical $350 million annual ceiling.

## Norway: The Residual Capex Obligation

The Mo i Rana CQP in Arctic Norway remained on T1 Energy's balance sheet through the snapshot date, representing both a residual capex legacy and a strategic option on battery cell manufacturing that the company had not formally abandoned. The facility's carrying value and associated decommissioning or maintenance obligations appear in T1 Energy's SEC filings; the capital required to advance Mo i Rana from its current Customer Qualification Plant configuration to any form of commercial production would be substantial — likely in the hundreds of millions of dollars — and the company's disclosed capital allocation priority had unmistakably shifted toward Wilmer.

The practical effect of maintaining the Norway assets is a modest but persistent drag on corporate resources — facility costs, a reduced Norwegian workforce, intellectual property licensing obligations to 24M Technologies — against the theoretical optionality of a future battery business. As of the frozen snapshot, T1 Energy had not formally divested Mo i Rana, but the strategic hierarchy was unambiguous: Wilmer first, Norway a distant and contingent second.

The contrast with the July 2021 SPAC vision could not be starker. FREYR Battery raised capital under the banner of Norwegian battery sovereignty and the green transition of European industrial regions. T1 Energy deploys that capital's successor — rebuilt through subsequent financing actions — in a Texas module assembly facility, earning its economics from a US tax credit framework that did not exist when Tom Einar Jensen founded the company in 2018. The corporate metamorphosis was complete; whether the financial architecture could support the ambition of the second act remained the central question for investors entering 2026.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## A Company That Defies Conventional Metrics

Valuing T1 Energy as of 23 May 2026 demands an analytical framework that standard income-statement multiples cannot provide. The company arrived at this snapshot date as a strategic-pivot equity in the middle of its first full ramp year at the Wilmer, Texas solar module facility — a business that did not exist on T1's books before the November 2024 Trina Solar acquisition closed. Trailing earnings per share reflected the costs of a company still building, not yet harvesting. Price-to-earnings ratios were negative or meaningless. The more instructive lenses were enterprise value against potential manufacturing capacity, forward EV-to-sales on a ramp-adjusted basis, and — critically — what the current share price implied about the market's confidence in T1 capturing Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credits at scale.

The company formerly known as FREYR Battery had listed via SPAC in July 2021 at a moment of peak enthusiasm for European battery cell manufacturing ambitions. The de-rating that followed the broader lithium-ion capital-intensity reckoning of 2022–2024 was severe and well-documented. What T1 entered 2026 with was not a valuation built on earnings power but one that was attempting to reprice a new thesis — domestic US solar module manufacturing backed by the Inflation Reduction Act's Section 45X per-watt credit structure — from a deeply discounted base.

## Current Market Positioning

FREYR Battery's share count had grown substantially through the SPAC era and subsequent at-the-market equity programs. Based on T1 Energy's most recent SEC filings available prior to the frozen snapshot, shares outstanding were in the range of 160–185 million, with diluted count potentially reaching 190–210 million inclusive of warrant overhang and employee equity programs. The exact figure requires confirmation against T1 Energy's Q1 2026 10-Q or most recent 8-K; this chapter reasons from that plausible range.

T1 Energy's shares traded in a broad band through early 2026 as investors assessed execution progress at Wilmer. At observed price ranges of approximately $4.50–$9.00 per share in the months preceding the snapshot, the implied market capitalisation ranged from roughly $800 million to $1.65 billion. Using a midpoint of $6.50 per share and 175 million shares outstanding implies a market cap of approximately $1.14 billion. Net debt position depended on the balance sheet treatment of Section 45X credit receivables and the draw on the company's term facility; enterprise value was likely in the $1.2–$1.5 billion range, acknowledging balance-sheet uncertainty.

The more analytically grounded multiple was EV per gigawatt of nameplate manufacturing capacity. At $1.35 billion enterprise value against the 5 GW Wilmer facility, T1 traded at approximately $270 million per GW. The theoretical 45X credit ceiling — $0.07 per watt across 5 GW of annual production equates to $350 million per year at full utilisation — meant the market was pricing the business at roughly 3.9 times the annualised maximum credit stream, before accounting for operating costs, module margin, or any residual value assigned to the Norwegian battery assets.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

| Company | Ticker | Market Cap (approx.) | EV/Fwd Sales | EV/GW Capacity | 45X / IRA Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| First Solar | FSLR | ~$20–25B | 4.5–6.5× | ~$2,500–3,000/kW | Full domestic manufacturer |
| Canadian Solar | CSIQ | ~$1.5–2.5B | 0.3–0.5× | N/A (global mixed) | Limited US domestic content |
| Array Technologies | ARRY | ~$1.5–2.5B | 1.5–2.5× | N/A (tracker, not module) | IRA domestic content beneficiary |
| Shoals Technologies | SHLS | ~$1.0–1.8B | 3.0–4.5× | N/A (EBOS components) | US-manufactured components |
| Nextracker | NXT | ~$3.5–5.0B | 2.5–3.5× | N/A (tracker, not module) | IRA domestic content beneficiary |
| **T1 Energy** | **TE** | **~$0.9–1.4B** | **NM (ramp year)** | **~$240–300/kW** | **Full 45X module manufacturer** |

*All market cap and multiple figures are approximate, derived from publicly available trading ranges and analyst estimates as of or near 23 May 2026. First Solar figures sourced from FSLR investor relations and consensus estimates; T1 Energy figures reasoned from share count and observed price range as described.*

The gap between First Solar and T1 Energy on an EV-per-GW basis was stark — an order-of-magnitude discount — reflecting First Solar's decade of profitable domestic manufacturing history, its vertically integrated CdTe technology moat, and its established utility-scale customer relationships. T1 Energy's discount represented both the discount for execution risk and the premium still available if the Wilmer ramp proved credible.

## Historical Re-Rating

The stock's journey from its SPAC-era peak tells the story of two distinct narrative collapses and one attempted reconstruction. FREYR Battery common shares touched approximately $15–18 per share in late 2021 during the SPAC euphoria wave that lifted nearly every announced clean-energy manufacturer regardless of near-term revenue visibility. By early 2024, following the Atlanta gigafactory scale-back, the battery industry capital reset, and the company's own admission that the Norwegian CQP timeline had slipped, shares had compressed to below $2.50 — an approximate 85 percent drawdown from the peak.

The Trina Solar acquisition announcement in November 2024 and the subsequent Q1 2025 rename to T1 Energy produced a partial recovery. The market was pricing the company as a different asset: no longer a speculative battery manufacturer burning Norwegian sovereign-adjacent capital, but a US solar module producer with an immediately operational facility, an IRA-backed revenue structure, and a demonstrably simpler capital story. By mid-2025, shares had recovered into the $4–7 range. That recovery, while meaningful, still left the stock at a fraction of its SPAC-era high — a re-rating driven by the new thesis rather than a rehabilitation of the old one.

## Intrinsic Value and the 45X Credit Framework

A simplified intrinsic-value framework for T1 Energy required anchoring to the 45X credit stream rather than to conventional free-cash-flow projections, because the company's near-term economics are structurally dependent on that government payment.

At 5 GW of nameplate capacity and $0.07 per watt, the theoretical maximum Section 45X module credit is $350 million annually. Assume a normalised operating cost structure for a single-facility US solar module manufacturer with a wage structure consistent with the Wilmer, Texas labour market and supply chain sourcing still partly dependent on imported cells — a structural limitation that constrained full 45X stack capture in FY2025. On that basis, net 45X credits actually realised in FY2025 were likely in the $100–180 million range, rising toward $200–280 million in FY2026 as cell domestication progressed.

A DCF anchored to $200 million in FY2026 45X credits growing at a modest 5 percent annually over five years, discounted at 12 percent to reflect small-cap execution risk, and terminal-valued at 8× EBITDA, produced an indicative intrinsic value range of $7.50–$11.00 per share — above the approximate midpoint market price as of the snapshot, suggesting the market was not fully pricing a successful ramp. That gap was the investable thesis, and its risk was the bear case.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

| Scenario | Key Assumption | Implied 2027E 45X Revenue | EV/Revenue Multiple | Implied Share Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bull** | 5 GW at 85% utilisation; domestic cell sourcing achieved; no Section 45X legislative erosion | ~$295M | 5× | $13–17 |
| **Base** | 3.5 GW effective utilisation; cell sourcing partially domestic; some customer concentration discount | ~$200M | 3.5× | $8–11 |
| **Bear** | Policy risk materialises (45X credit phase-down or tariff shock to cell inputs); 2.0 GW effective utilisation; equity dilution | ~$100M | 2× | $3–5 |

The bull case required T1 to close the cell-domestication gap — sourcing cells from a US-manufactured or domestically-treated supply chain to capture the full 45X stack rather than the module-only credit. It also assumed no legislative erosion of the IRA Section 45X framework through the congressional budget process that remained active through the snapshot window. The base case was consistent with an orderly Wilmer ramp and mid-cycle normalised operations. The bear case reflected the combination of IRA credit uncertainty — a recurring risk for the entire US solar manufacturing sector in 2025–2026 given congressional budget discussions — and T1's specific execution risk as a single-facility operator with a Norwegian battery legacy complicating its investor narrative.

## What the Market Is Pricing In

As of the frozen snapshot, the consensus appeared to be anchored somewhere between the bear and base scenarios — pricing in successful Wilmer operation at reduced utilisation, with a meaningful policy-risk discount embedded in the multiple. The stock was not pricing a bull outcome, and it was not pricing a catastrophic 45X unwinding. It was pricing *uncertainty about the ramp and the regulatory durability of the credit regime*.

The dossier's read diverged modestly from that consensus in one direction: the market appeared to be assigning insufficient weight to the strategic option value embedded in the Wilmer facility's scalability and in T1's positioning as one of only a handful of US-domiciled solar module manufacturers capable of offering utility-scale buyers domestically manufactured product at gigawatt scale. First Solar could not satisfy all demand; T1's Wilmer capacity was a real industrial asset in a market structurally short of qualifying supply. That scarcity premium — not fully reflected in a $270 million per GW EV — was the dossier's primary point of constructive differentiation from the consensus bear posture.

chapters.title: Pre-pivot FREYR quarters through Trina acquisition and post-rename ramp
chapters.body:
## The Battery Thesis, Intact — Until It Wasn't

When FREYR AS closed its business combination with Alussa Energy Acquisition Corp. on July 9, 2021, the Norwegian lithium-ion startup arrived on the New York Stock Exchange with a pro forma equity value of $1.4 billion, a $600 million PIPE, and a thesis premised on the conviction that clean battery cell manufacturing — anchored in Norway's hydropower grid — could be scaled into a globally competitive enterprise. Ticker: FREY. The ambition was explicit: FREYR would build Giga Arctic in Mo i Rana, Norway, using the licensed 24M Technologies SemiSolid™ platform, and pair it with an American manufacturing footprint that would leverage the Inflation Reduction Act's incentive architecture. In November 2022 the company announced the purchase of a 368-acre site in Coweta County, Georgia — Giga America — with an initial capital investment estimate of $1.7 billion and a preliminary target of 34 GWh of annual cell production capacity.

The quarterly cadence through 2022 and into 2023 tracked two parallel narratives: progress at the Customer Qualification Plant in Mo i Rana, and capital planning for the Georgia site. Neither moved as fast as the equity story had promised. For the full year ended December 31, 2022, FREYR reported a net loss of $98.8 million, or $0.83 per diluted share, with revenue still effectively nil. The company had capital but no product. In the background, the Inflation Reduction Act's Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credits had passed in August 2022 — initially designed to accelerate domestic US battery cell production — but the same legislation that was meant to validate FREYR's US expansion simultaneously recalibrated the calculus for Norwegian manufacturing. A $35-per-kWh production tax credit available to US-made lithium-ion cells made it materially harder to justify the capital intensity of a European gigafactory. The IRA had, in the words of one company executive at the time, "shifted the market."

## The C-Suite Revolving Door

The strategic tension produced leadership turbulence. In August 2023 the company announced that co-founder and chief executive Tom Einar Jensen would become Executive Chair, with Birger Steen — a technology sector veteran with stints leading Microsoft's operations in Norway and Russia — installed as CEO. Torstein Dale Sjøtveit, FREYR's founding Executive Chair, retired on the same date. Steen lasted ten months. By June 2024, Jensen was reinstated as chief executive, Steen departed from both the CEO seat and the board, and Daniel Barcelo — a director on the FREYR board — was elevated to Chair. Evan Calio was named CFO concurrently. The whipsaw succession reflected something deeper than personality conflict: the company's strategic center of gravity was still in motion.

For the full year ended December 31, 2023, FREYR reported a net loss of $71.9 million, or $0.51 per diluted share — a narrowing versus 2022 that reflected aggressive cost rationalisation rather than revenue progress. Year-end cash stood at $276 million. Management projected a two-year liquidity runway on a reduced-burn basis. The Giga America capex estimate had by then grown to $2.6 billion; the Giga Arctic milestone targets had been quietly pushed back. In Norway, 78 employees and contractors were laid off as part of a restructuring that cut the management layer from 19 directors to six. The company described its posture as "FREYR 2.0" — a pivot to the US market — though the specific vector of that pivot remained undefined.

## Barcelo Takes Command

The definition arrived in the autumn of 2024. In a leadership configuration change that preceded the company's most consequential transaction, Daniel Barcelo assumed the chief executive role from Jensen, who was appointed CEO of FREYR Europe to oversee the "optimization and monetization" of the European portfolio — a diplomatic formulation for an orderly wind-down. The transition positioned Barcelo as the executive who would execute the strategic break.

On November 6, 2024, FREYR announced the acquisition of Trina Solar's US manufacturing assets: a 5 GW, 1.35-million-square-foot solar module manufacturing facility in Wilmer, Texas — subsequently branded G1 Dallas — for total consideration of $340 million to Trina, structured as $100 million in cash, a $50 million repayment of an intercompany loan, $150 million in senior preferred notes, and equity comprising 9.9% of FREYR's outstanding common stock at closing plus a convertible instrument converting into an additional 11.5%. Trina Solar retained approximately 17.4% of T1 equity post-transaction and board representation.

> "We are pleased to announce this transformative transaction, which will immediately position the Company as one of the leading solar manufacturing companies in the U.S. We are proud to be partnered with Trina Solar, a global manufacturing and solar technology leader," said Barcelo at the announcement. "Domestic manufacturing capacity for solar and batteries is essential for energy transition and job creation. The U.S. was once the global leader in solar, and it can be again."

The Wilmer facility had commenced production on November 1, 2024 — five days before the announcement. Line 1 was operational; commissioning on Line 2 had begun. The full seven-line facility was targeting production ramp through H2 2025. Thirty percent of estimated production volumes were backed by firm US customer offtake contracts. The transaction closed on December 24, 2024.

## The Rename and the Reckoning with Georgia

Barcelo's strategic reorientation completed its symbolic arc on February 19, 2025, when the company filed to change its corporate name from FREYR Battery Inc. to **T1 Energy Inc.** Common stock and warrants ceased trading under FREY and FREY WS on March 3, 2025, and commenced as TE and TE WS on the New York Stock Exchange. Headquarters relocated from Houston to Austin, Texas.

Nine days before the rename, on February 10, 2025, came the formal admission that Giga America was finished. The company announced the sale of its Coweta County, Georgia site to an undisclosed buyer for gross proceeds of $50 million — netting $22.5 million after repayment of state and local grants. The project, which had grown from a $1.7 billion original plan to a $2.6 billion total investment estimate, was attributed by the company to "rising interest rates, falling battery prices, changes in management, and a realignment of the company's near-term strategic goals." The six-year battery cell chapter was closed.

> "The rebirth of our company as T1 Energy is about American energy, jobs, and advanced manufacturing. The U.S. needs domestic supply chains and manufacturing capacity to harness its abundant solar resources. T1 is committed to building that capacity," Barcelo said at the rename. "More than 80% of new U.S. electricity capacity in 2024 was solar and batteries. T1 plans to lead in the solar and battery markets by enabling the growth in energy supply required to support AI, data centers, reshoring, and electrification — to restore American industrial capacity and leadership in future advanced industries."

## Post-Rename Ramp: The First Year

FY2024 had recorded only $2.9 million in consolidated revenue against a net loss of $450.2 million — the bulk of the loss attributable to pre-acquisition wind-down costs and the Norwegian portfolio write-downs. The first full quarter as T1 Energy showed what the Wilmer asset could do: in Q1 2025, G1 Dallas produced 443 MW of solar modules, representing 96% of the company's internal production plan, and generated $64.6 million in revenue exclusively from deliveries under the inherited Trina offtake contract.

The trajectory was constructive but complicated. In mid-2025, T1 revised its full-year production plan downward from 3.4 GW to 2.6–3.0 GW, citing the need to accommodate trade and industrial policy uncertainty, production line technology conversions, and the ramp of new sales initiatives beyond the Trina offtake. For the full year 2025, the company delivered 2.79 GW of modules and $755.3 million in revenue — a near-vertical inflection from the pre-acquisition baseline — against a net loss of $380.8 million and an adjusted EBITDA of negative $65.0 million. Year-end unrestricted cash was $182.5 million.

The IRA Section 45X credit was already showing up in the financial architecture. T1 monetised $160 million of 45X production tax credits during 2025, selling them at $0.91 on the dollar — a haircut typical of the nascent transferability market, but meaningful cashflow against a manufacturing cost base still absorbing ramp inefficiencies. At $0.07 per watt for modules, the 5 GW facility represents a theoretical credit entitlement of approximately $350 million per year at full utilisation — a figure that frames the company's economic proposition to the patient capital it will need to complete the transition.

| Period | Revenue (USD) | Net Loss (USD) | Module Production |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | Negligible | $98.8M | — (battery CQP) |
| FY2023 | Negligible | $71.9M | — (battery CQP) |
| FY2024 | $2.9M | $450.2M | Transition year |
| Q1 2025 | $64.6M | — | 443 MW |
| FY2025 | $755.3M | $380.8M | 2.79 GW |

> "2025 was a defining year for T1 Energy as we advanced our strategy to build the U.S. solar platform," Barcelo said in the FY2025 earnings release. The company entered 2026 guiding production of 3.1 to 4.2 GW and targeting a G2 domestic cell manufacturing facility — site selection completed in Q1 2025, construction originally targeted mid-2025 — that would deepen the vertical integration story FREYR's Norwegian founders once told about batteries.

---

**Sources:** [FREYR Battery / T1 Energy IR press releases](https://ir.t1energy.com) · [SEC EDGAR filings (CIK 0001992243)](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001992243) · [Trina acquisition closing announcement](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-closes-transformative-acquisition-trina-solars-us) · [T1 Energy rebrand press release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-rebrands-t1-energy) · [FREYR Battery FQ4 2023 results, BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240229252927/en/FREYR-Battery-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2023-Results) · [Giga America cancellation, ESS News](https://www.ess-news.com/2025/02/10/freyr-cancels-2-6-billion-gigafactory-in-georgia-sells-site/) · [PV Magazine rebrand coverage](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2025/02/20/freyr-battery-rebrands-as-ti-energy-relocates-to-austin/) · [StockTitan FY2025 results summary](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/TE/8-k-t1-energy-inc-reports-material-event-6ecfab1d447a.html) · [Alussa SPAC merger, BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20210630005988/en/Alussa-Energy-Acquisition-Corp.-Shareholders-Approve-Business-Combination-with-FREYR-AS)

chapters.title: Daniel Barcelo, Trina-inherited operational leadership, and the post-rename board
chapters.body:
## From Founder to Subsidiary: Tom Einar Jensen's Receding Arc

When FREYR Battery went public via the Alussa Energy SPAC in July 2021, Tom Einar Jensen was the face and founding logic of the enterprise — a Norwegian entrepreneur whose conviction that Arctic hydropower could sustain a world-scale battery cell manufacturer had attracted sovereign fund interest and considerable equity capital from Oslo to New York. Jensen had co-founded FREYR AS in 2018 alongside Torstein Dale Sjøtveit, who retired from the company's leadership in the course of the 2023 succession that would mark the beginning of FREYR's long leadership turbulence.

The battery industry's capital-intensity reset, gathering force through 2022 and 2023, made Jensen's CEO position progressively untenable. In August 2023, he transitioned to Executive Chair of the Board, and Birger Steen — a Norwegian technology-sector executive — was brought in to execute what the board described as an accelerated path toward profitability. Steen lasted ten months. In June 2024, with the company still searching for a route to cash-flow-positive battery operations, Steen and CFO Oscar Brown departed within hours of each other. Steen's exit was framed by the board in purely strategic terms — the need to [accelerate] profitability — while Brown cited personal circumstances. Both had received substantial executive packages; Steen alone collected a NOK 7 million severance.

Jensen returned to the CEO role in June 2024 on an interim basis while the board simultaneously restructured its own upper tier. Daniel Barcelo was appointed Chair. Evan Calio was named CFO. The arrangement was understood by the market as a bridge position: Jensen was the continuity vehicle while the board negotiated the Trina Solar asset acquisition that would define the company's subsequent identity.

When the Trina deal was announced November 5, 2024, Barcelo was installed as CEO the following day. Jensen's institutional role at the NYSE-listed parent was then resolved: he stepped down from the T1 Energy board and accepted the position of CEO of FREYR Europe, the subsidiary retaining oversight of the Mo i Rana battery cell assets in Norway. His shareholding — approximately 2.8 million shares carried through the transition — maintained financial alignment with the renamed enterprise even as his operating authority narrowed to what had become, deliberately, the lower-priority portfolio.

## Daniel Barcelo: Capital-Markets Operator in a Manufacturing Chair

Barcelo, 56 at the time of his November 2024 appointment, arrived at T1 Energy's executive office via energy finance rather than energy production. He had been a portfolio manager at Moore Capital Management, one of the pre-crisis era's most prominent macro hedge funds. Before Moore, he served as a Senior Research Analyst in oil and gas at Bank of America, and as a Director and Senior Analyst in the same sector at Lehman Brothers. A tenure as Managing Director and Head of Oil and Gas at Renaissance Capital in Moscow gave him direct exposure to the Russian energy complex at a moment of peak Western institutional interest in that market.

Barcelo also held operating-level financial roles: Chief Financial Officer of Ruspetro plc, a Russia-focused upstream oil producer listed in London; Head of Corporate Finance at Lekoil Limited, an E&P company active in Nigeria; co-founder and CFO of Invicti Terra Argentina Limited, a Latin American energy development vehicle. He is a CFA charterholder with a BS in Finance from Syracuse University.

At T1 Energy, that résumé maps most directly to the single most consequential near-term management challenge: not manufacturing yield optimization but the monetization of Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credits — a structured-finance exercise requiring credibility with institutional tax-equity buyers. The first $160 million sale of Section 45X credits, completed at $0.91 per dollar, came out in the full-year 2025 results. Barcelo's public statements since the rename have consistently framed T1's thesis in supply-chain integration terms rather than module-level cost competition:

> "We are building something that does not exist in the U.S. today — an integrated, secure, traceable polysilicon-based supply chain."

At the March 2026 earnings release, covering the 2025 full year, he described the period with the kind of summarizing confidence that suggests the manufacturing ramp met internal expectations:

> "2025 was a defining year for T1 Energy as we advanced our strategy to build America's first vertically integrated, silicon-based solar platform."

## Joseph Evan Calio: The CFO Pairing

Joseph Evan Calio, appointed CFO on June 13, 2024, as part of the same leadership reset that brought Barcelo to Chair, carried a career trajectory that closely paralleled his CEO's. Calio had been a Managing Director covering Energy and Infrastructure investment banking at BTIG; before that, he spent fourteen years at Morgan Stanley as a Managing Director in equity research covering E&P companies, refiners, and integrated oils. He holds a BS from Lehigh University, a JD from Widener University School of Law, and an LLM from Georgetown University Law Center — a combination suggesting the tax and structured-finance literacy that T1's Section 45X credit sales will continue to demand. Calio received a 666,666 RSU grant vesting ratably over three years, anchoring his economic interest through the stated 2027 operational target of 5 GW of integrated production between the G1 Dallas and G2 Austin facilities.

## Operational Continuity: The FREYR Engineering Thread

One executive who bridged the Norwegian founding and the Texas build-out was Einar GS Kilde, who had served as Chief Operating Officer of FREYR AS since October 2019 — predating the SPAC listing and representing the deepest institutional memory of the Mo i Rana construction years. His title evolved to Chief Development Officer as the company's capital deployment shifted to the G2 Austin solar cell facility. He retired from T1 Energy in April 2026, closing out the last of the original FREYR engineering leadership from the parent-company executive suite.

Beneath that layer, Barcelo assembled a functional team that included Jaime Gualy as Executive Vice President of Corporate Development, Andy Munro as Chief Legal Officer, and Russell Gold as Executive Vice President of Strategic Communications — a configuration reflecting both the external presentation demands of a post-SPAC NYSE company and the specific Washington visibility that an IRA-era domestic manufacturing story commands.

## Board Architecture: Holdovers, the Trina Designee, and the Post-Rename Refresh

The board T1 Energy carried through the February 2025 rename was predominantly a FREYR Battery–era construction. The nine directors elected at the June 2025 annual meeting included the chairman-CEO Barcelo and a contingent of independent directors whose appointments traced to the 2021–2024 FREYR period.

| Director | Background | Board tenure origin |
|---|---|---|
| Daniel Barcelo | Moore Capital / Lehman / Ruspetro CFO; Chairman & CEO | Nov. 2024 (appointment as CEO) |
