chapters.title: US solar developers, polysilicon and wafer supply, and the Norway battery upstream
chapters.body:
## The Customer Base: US Utility-Scale Solar

The 5-gigawatt Wilmer manufacturing plant that T1 Energy acquired from Trina Solar in November 2024 is, at its most fundamental level, a bet on the continued expansion of US utility-scale solar installation. Located in a suburb of Dallas and configured for the monocrystalline PERC and TOPCon module formats that dominate utility procurement specifications, the facility supplies a customer base drawn principally from the US independent power producer community — project sponsors and engineering, procurement, and construction contractors for whom IRA domestic content eligibility is a material project-finance consideration.

The structural commercial driver is the domestic content bonus adder under Sections 48 and 45Y of the IRA: projects qualifying under Treasury's domestic content guidance for steel, iron, and manufactured products access an additional 10-percentage-point bonus on the base tax credit, with a further pathway available under defined circumstances. For a utility-scale project financed on tax-equity terms, that adder materially reshapes project IRRs. T1 Energy's Wilmer-manufactured modules are positioned — subject to the cell content rules discussed below — to qualify as US-manufactured products for this purpose, creating a direct commercial link between the IRA's domestic content incentive architecture and Wilmer's order book.

The broader utility-scale US solar installation pipeline ran at roughly 30 GW annually through 2024-2025, with First Solar's Series 6 and Series 7 thin-film product dominating the domestically manufactured segment. T1 Energy enters a market where First Solar has historically extracted premium pricing on the strength of its domestic manufacturing and FEOC-compliant supply chain, and where the primary pricing competition for crystalline silicon modules originates from Southeast Asian producers navigating an increasingly litigated trade environment. Beyond utility-scale developers, the Wilmer facility's module specifications are compatible with commercial and community solar applications, though the company's disclosed commercial focus has centred on the large-project procurement channel where domestic content value is most directly monetised.

## Polysilicon and Wafer: The China Upstream Dependency

The critical upstream constraint at Wilmer is cells and wafers. Standard crystalline silicon module manufacturing requires a supply chain running from polysilicon through ingot to wafer to cell before module assembly — and as of the Trina acquisition, Wilmer was configured for module assembly, not cell production. Cell procurement is therefore the decisive upstream exposure.

China accounts for roughly 80-90 percent of global polysilicon, wafer, and cell manufacturing capacity. The leading Chinese cell producers — Tongwei, LONGi Green Energy, JA Solar, and Trina Solar itself — operate at cost structures that nascent US-based cell manufacturing cannot yet replicate at comparable scale absent subsidy support. The IRA's Section 45X advanced manufacturing production credit partially addresses this: at $0.04 per watt for solar cells and $0.07 per watt for completed modules, the credit establishes an economic floor for domestic cell production. The problem is that sufficient US cell capacity to supply a 5 GW module facility at full utilisation does not yet exist.

The US polysilicon base remains thin. Hemlock Semiconductor, headquartered in Hemlock, Michigan, is the primary domestic polysilicon producer, serving both semiconductor-grade and solar end markets. REC Silicon — the Norwegian polysilicon manufacturer with a facility in Butte, Montana — has faced recurring operational constraints tied to the same trade dynamics that hollowed out US solar upstream economics during 2018-2022. Neither producer offers polysilicon at the scale or pricing comparable to Chinese counterparts, and no meaningful vertically integrated ingot, wafer, or cell manufacturing capacity exists in the US today at the volume T1 Energy would require.

| Upstream input | Current US capacity | Key domestic suppliers | Estimated China global share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Polysilicon | Limited | Hemlock Semiconductor; REC Silicon (Butte, MT) | ~85% |
| Ingot / Wafer | Minimal | — | ~95%+ |
| Solar cells | Early-stage | Hanwha Q CELLS (Dalton, GA); planned expansions | ~85% |
| Modules | Growing | First Solar; T1 Energy/Wilmer; Hanwha Q CELLS; Silfab | Expanding US share post-IRA |

For T1 Energy, building an IRA-compliant and FEOC-clean upstream supply chain over the medium term means either sourcing cells from the small number of US cell manufacturers, contracting with non-FEOC-designated country suppliers — Hanwha Q CELLS' Dalton, Georgia cell facility is the most significant non-Chinese domestic cell source — or procuring through Southeast Asian or Indian producers whose supply chains can satisfy the domestic content test for the module bonus adder in the near-term transition period. The latter is the most operationally realistic near-term procurement pathway at scale, though it carries trade litigation exposure.

## The Trina Solar Relationship: Former Parent, Technology Licensor, Residual Supplier

The November 2024 acquisition transferred Trina Solar's Wilmer operations to what was then FREYR Battery, subsequently T1 Energy, but the commercial and technical relationship between buyer and former parent did not sever cleanly at closing. Trina Solar retained its global manufacturing operations, technology platform, and brand; what transferred was the US manufacturing footprint and associated assets. Transition services agreements customary in carve-out transactions would govern near-term operational continuity across manufacturing processes, supply logistics, and technical support.

The cell supply question intersects directly with the Trina relationship in a manner that creates ongoing compliance complexity. If Trina Solar remained a cell supplier to Wilmer post-acquisition — a logical short-term arrangement given established supply relationships at the facility — the arrangement would expose T1 Energy to the same Chinese supply chain risk that constrains IRA domestic content eligibility and raises FEOC exposure as Treasury and DOE tighten the foreign entity of concern rules applicable to solar and battery components. Trina Solar's corporate structure and any PRC state-linked ownership interests are a material due diligence variable for any sustained cell procurement arrangement involving Trina-affiliated entities.

T1 Energy's management has publicly characterised the Wilmer facility as targeting a domestically compliant supply chain over time. The transition period implies a managed migration away from Chinese-origin cell supply rather than an immediate severance — a trajectory that parallels the IRA's own phase-in schedule for FEOC restrictions, which tighten progressively through the mid-2020s.

## US-China Trade Policy: Tariff Architecture and UFLPA Exposure

The US solar import tariff regime has been in effective force since the Obama administration's antidumping and countervailing duty orders on Chinese crystalline silicon products, with the Section 201 safeguard tariff layer added in January 2018. The Biden administration largely maintained the architecture while adding complexity: a June 2022 presidential proclamation waived Section 201 tariffs on imports from Malaysia, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Thailand for 24 months to address near-term supply shortages, while simultaneously initiating circumvention investigations into whether Chinese manufacturers were routing production through those countries to evade existing US orders.

The framework entering T1 Energy's 2025 operational period was one in which cells and modules of Chinese origin — or of Southeast Asian origin adjudged to circumvent existing orders — faced combined AD/CVD and Section 201 duty exposure exceeding 40-50 percent across most product categories. The Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, effective June 2022, layered a rebuttable presumption of forced labour for goods with any Xinjiang nexus; a substantial proportion of Chinese polysilicon has historically been produced in or processed through Xinjiang, creating documentary compliance requirements that Chinese suppliers have been inconsistent in satisfying.

For T1 Energy, this tariff and compliance environment simultaneously constitutes the economic moat supporting Wilmer's viability and the supply chain constraint limiting upstream optionality. Domestically manufactured modules avoid tariff burden and UFLPA exposure entirely. The constraint is procuring upstream inputs — cells above all — at competitive cost while maintaining the supply chain traceability documentation that IRA compliance and UFLPA enforcement require.

## Norway: The Battery Upstream That Persists

T1 Energy's Norway operations — principally the Mo i Rana Customer Qualification Plant representing FREYR Battery's original lithium-ion manufacturing thesis — continued under the renamed entity at reduced strategic priority through the period under review. The CQP was designed to demonstrate FREYR's licensed manufacturing technology, sourced from 24M Technologies of Cambridge, Massachusetts, and to qualify prospective customers for larger-scale Norwegian cell supply. Capital deployment toward Wilmer through 2025 placed Mo i Rana on a maintenance trajectory rather than an active investment path.

The battery upstream exposure at Mo i Rana is structurally analogous to Wilmer's solar supply challenge: lithium, nickel, manganese, and cobalt for NMC chemistry cells are similarly concentrated in supply chains with dominant Chinese processing. The IRA's FEOC restrictions, applied to battery components under Section 45X and Section 48C, create parallel sourcing constraints to those facing solar upstream, with tightening schedules that make non-Chinese battery raw material supply increasingly necessary for credit eligibility. FREYR's original Norwegian manufacturing thesis had anticipated leveraging Norway's renewable energy cost advantage and proximity to European battery supply chains; the strategic pivot to US solar effectively suspended that thesis without formally abandoning it.

The Norway assets represent, in the post-rename context, an optionality position on a battery market recovery rather than an active capital deployment programme — retaining residual value as a developed industrial site with existing regulatory approvals, without commanding meaningful near-term investment priority against Wilmer's Section 45X-supported economics.

chapters.title: Where T1 Energy sits against First Solar and the US solar module manufacturing build-out
chapters.body:
The US solar module manufacturing landscape that T1 Energy entered through its November 2024 acquisition of Trina Solar's Wilmer, Texas operations was not a greenfield opportunity. By the time FREYR Battery completed its rebranding as T1 Energy in early 2025, the field already had a clear dominant player, a cohort of well-capitalized Korean-backed entrants, and a policy architecture — IRA Section 45X — that had reshaped the economics of domestic production in ways that rewarded incumbency. The question for T1 was not whether US solar manufacturing had a future; that debate was largely settled. The question was whether a company with a roughly $100–200 million entry ticket and a 5-gigawatt facility originally built by one of China's largest panel producers could carve out defensible ground against competitors with far longer US manufacturing histories and, in at least one case, meaningfully different technology.

## First Solar: The Benchmark No One Touches

No analysis of US solar module manufacturing begins anywhere other than First Solar. The Tempe, Arizona–headquartered company spent the better part of two decades building a cadmium-telluride thin-film manufacturing capability that no competitor has replicated at commercial scale. By the time IRA Section 45X took effect, First Solar was already generating advanced manufacturing production credits on a production base expanding toward and beyond 10 gigawatts of annual US nameplate capacity, distributed across facilities in Perrysburg, Ohio — which operates multiple sequential plants — and a newer Alabama factory that came online in 2024. The company's thin-film technology is proprietary and structurally differentiated from the crystalline-silicon modules that dominate global trade: CdTe panels carry temperature coefficients that perform advantageously at utility-scale installations in high-irradiance, high-heat US markets, and they carry no exposure to the polysilicon supply chains that have drawn Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act scrutiny since the law's 2022 implementation.

First Solar's balance sheet entering 2025 reflected those advantages. The company had accumulated substantial Section 45X credit flows while carrying a net cash position that gave it financial flexibility no new entrant could match. Its customer roster was dominated by long-duration utility-scale power purchase agreements with investment-grade offtakers — the kind of contracts that emerge from years of bankability track record rather than a single acquisition. For T1 Energy, First Solar represented the ceiling of what US-headquartered solar module manufacturing could aspire to, and a competitor effectively impossible to displace from the upper utility-scale tier without a decade-long operational history of its own.

## The Korean Entrants and the Crystalline-Silicon Field

T1 Energy's more immediate competitive universe was the cluster of crystalline-silicon module manufacturers who, like it, were producing n-type TOPCon or PERC-architecture panels and drawing on 45X credits to bridge the cost gap with overseas production. Hanwha Q CELLS, the US subsidiary of South Korea's Hanwha Solutions, committed roughly $2.5 billion to a Cartersville, Georgia facility that scaled toward approximately 8 gigawatts of annual module capacity through 2024 and 2025. Hanwha brought Korean balance-sheet depth, existing utility-scale customer relationships built over years of US distribution, and the ability to integrate a domestic cell manufacturing line that unlocked the cell-level 45X credit on top of the module-level credit. That stacked credit capture — $0.04 per watt for cells plus $0.07 per watt for modules — was a meaningful economics differentiator for manufacturers able to produce both, compared with those assembling modules from imported cells.

Silfab Solar, the Canadian-headquartered manufacturer with US production in Monroe, Washington and additional North American sites, operated at smaller scale but with established Pacific Northwest customer relationships and a manufacturing pedigree that predated the IRA incentive cycle. Heliene, another Canadian-headquartered producer, similarly held US production positions. Further down the capacity curve, a broader cohort of announced US manufacturing projects — some from Chinese-parent companies seeking to establish tariff-advantaged US entities, others from novel entrants — was navigating an uncertain regulatory environment as Treasury issued domestic content bonus adder guidance and Commerce continued anti-circumvention proceedings against Southeast Asian production by Chinese-owned entities.

## T1's Inherited Footprint and the Trina Provenance Question

T1 Energy's Wilmer, Texas facility entered the competitive landscape with a specific heritage that shaped both its opportunities and its vulnerabilities. The plant was purpose-built by Trina Solar — one of the world's largest solar module producers by global shipment volume — to serve US customers from a domestically domiciled production base. Trina's decision to divest the facility rather than continue operating it through a trade-sensitive period reflected a calculation about the complexity of Chinese-parent-company exposure under an increasingly stringent US trade and investment review framework. For FREYR Battery — then in the late stages of its strategic pivot away from the Norwegian battery thesis — acquiring the Wilmer plant offered a path to overnight relevance in US advanced manufacturing.

The 5-gigawatt nameplate at Wilmer was substantial on paper. It positioned T1, at full run-rate, as the second-largest US solar module manufacturer by stated capacity — a striking fact for a company that had been a Norwegian battery startup eighteen months prior. But nameplate capacity and actual shipped gigawatts are distinct quantities. As of the snapshot date, T1 was in the process of ramping production at Wilmer rather than operating at full utilization. The facility's production economics, and therefore its actual 45X credit capture, were a function of utilization rates that had not yet reached levels commensurate with the cash flows implied by a fully loaded 5-gigawatt production scenario.

## Technology: TOPCon Against the Field

The Wilmer facility produced TOPCon modules — n-type tunnel-oxide passivated contact architecture — which represented the leading edge of crystalline-silicon efficiency in commercial production as of 2025. TOPCon offered efficiency advantages over the older PERC architecture that had dominated global shipments through the early 2020s, and T1's Trina-derived production capability theoretically placed it at the higher-efficiency end of the crystalline-silicon competitive set. Against First Solar's CdTe differentiation, the comparison was less clear; thin-film and crystalline-silicon address slightly different market niches and project-financing frameworks, leaving headroom for both technology families in the utility-scale buildout.

| Manufacturer | Technology | Approx. US Capacity (GW) | Domestic Cell Production |
|---|---|---|---|
| First Solar | CdTe thin-film | ~10+ | Yes (integrated) |
| Hanwha Q CELLS | TOPCon / PERC | ~8 | Yes (Cartersville) |
| T1 Energy | TOPCon | ~5 | No |
| Silfab Solar | Mono PERC / TOPCon | ~2 | Limited |

The absence of domestic cell production at Wilmer was a competitive gap with direct financial consequences. US TOPCon cells were in constrained domestic supply, leaving T1 dependent on imported cells — from Trina Solar's global production network or alternative suppliers — to feed the Wilmer assembly lines. That dependency had two compounding effects: it reduced 45X credit capture to the module level only, and it created supply-chain exposure to any additional trade actions targeting cell imports from the Asian markets dominating cell production. The module-level 45X credit of $0.07 per watt translated, at 5 gigawatts of full production, to approximately $350 million in annual credit value — a number that clarified why the facility existed and why FREYR Battery had pursued the acquisition. A domestic cell line, had one existed, would have added a further $200 million at full run-rate, underscoring the gap between T1's current configuration and the vertically integrated economics Hanwha was assembling in Georgia.

## The 45X Equalizer and the Trade Policy Moat

Section 45X was, above all else, the reason the US solar module manufacturing competitive landscape looked as it did entering 2025. The advanced manufacturing production credit made domestic production economics viable at a time when Chinese manufacturers — absent the tariff and trade-remedy exposure that blocked their direct US market access — could produce modules at costs that no US facility with American-scale labor and regulatory compliance costs could approach in a purely market-driven framework. For all the competitive differences between First Solar's proprietary thin-film technology and Hanwha's stacked-credit TOPCon modules and T1's Wilmer facility, the 45X credit was the shared foundation on which each company's US manufacturing business case rested.

That shared dependency was also a shared policy risk. The IRA Section 45X credit was written through 2032, with phase-downs beginning in 2030, but the legislative and regulatory environment around advanced manufacturing incentives remained subject to political change. For T1 Energy — a company that had staked its entire post-pivot strategic identity on the November 2024 Trina acquisition and the 45X-supported US solar manufacturing thesis — that policy dependency was not an abstraction. It was the governing variable of the investment case, as exposed to Washington as to Wilmer.

chapters.title: From 2018 founding through SPAC, Atlanta reset, Trina, and T1 rename
chapters.body:
## The Norwegian Founding and the Battery Bet

FREYR Battery was incorporated in 2018 by Norwegian entrepreneur Tom Einar Jensen, who had identified a European strategic gap: the continent's automotive and grid-storage industries were building out demand for electric-vehicle and stationary battery cells at an accelerating pace, yet lithium-ion manufacturing capacity remained concentrated in East Asia. Jensen's thesis was geopolitical as much as industrial — establish a vertically integrated battery gigafactory in Norway, leveraging the country's abundant hydropower-sourced electricity, its established heavy-industrial workforce in the Arctic north, and the supply-chain provenance premium that European original equipment manufacturers were beginning to attach to domestically sourced cells.

The chosen site was Mo i Rana, a small industrial city in Nordland county with a history in steel and aluminium smelting, cheap and renewable power, port access, and a municipal government eager to attract next-generation manufacturing investment. The company was registered in Luxembourg — a structure that gave it European legal standing and capital market optionality — while retaining its operational and cultural identity as a Norwegian enterprise.

## The SPAC Window and the NYSE Listing

By mid-2021, the blank-check merger wave was at its apex, and clean-energy manufacturing concepts ranked among its most enthusiastic beneficiaries. FREYR Battery completed its merger with Alussa Energy Acquisition Corp in July 2021 and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker FREY. The transaction valued the company at approximately $1.4 billion and delivered gross proceeds intended to fund construction of a Customer Qualification Plant at Mo i Rana — which would produce sample cells for prospective industrial customers — and eventually a commercial-scale "Giga Arctic" facility on the same site.

The SPAC route gave FREYR access to US equity capital at a moment when investors were prepared to underwrite pre-revenue manufacturing concepts on the strength of long-range energy transition projections. The company's investor presentations leaned heavily on Mo i Rana's renewable energy cost advantage and projected a multi-gigawatt production ramp extending into the mid-2020s. The Luxembourg holding structure and the New York listing formed the bridge between a Norwegian industrial thesis and an American growth-equity investor base.

## Mo i Rana, Atlanta, and the Capital Intensity Reckoning

The Mo i Rana CQP entered construction in 2022. Concurrently, FREYR announced ambitions to develop a US gigafactory near Atlanta, Georgia — a move partly prompted by the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act in August 2022 and the advanced manufacturing incentives embedded in its domestic production credit architecture.

But the broader battery manufacturing industry was already repricing its assumptions. The capital cost of greenfield lithium-ion cell production — demanding ultra-clean room environments, precision formation cycling equipment, and tight upstream supply chain integration — proved substantially more consuming than SPAC-era projections had allowed. Asian incumbent manufacturers, with amortised tooling and consolidated supply chains accumulated over a decade of scale investment, held structural cost advantages that greenfield Western entrants could not close quickly through capital spending alone. By 2023, multiple European and North American battery manufacturing ventures were revisiting their volume and timeline commitments.

FREYR scaled back its Atlanta gigafactory plans. The Mo i Rana CQP remained the company's principal operational asset, but its commercial pathway — qualifying cells at volumes sufficient to attract binding customer offtake — was proving materially slower than investor-deck timelines had implied.

## The Barcelo Succession and the Strategic Reset

Tom Einar Jensen, FREYR's founding chief executive, departed during the 2023–2024 strategic reset period. Daniel Barcelo succeeded him as CEO, inheriting a listed company with a functioning qualification facility in northern Norway, a challenged equity valuation, and an urgent mandate to identify a strategic posture that could credibly close the gap between capital markets expectations and operational reality.

Barcelo's assessment was methodical. The battery manufacturing thesis was not without merit at a concept level — Mo i Rana CQP was producing cells, and demand for European-provenance battery supply was genuine. But the capital intensity of scaling from qualification to full commercial production, absent a committed large-volume customer willing to provide co-investment or binding long-term offtake, was a structural obstacle that the company's balance sheet could not absorb independently.

By the middle of 2024, the strategic aperture had widened. If the company's core institutional competency was navigating the US and European energy-transition policy incentive architecture — understanding how to position manufacturing assets to capture tax credits and advanced manufacturing support — then a different underlying technology could carry that competency forward.

## The Trina Acquisition: Pivoting to US Solar

In November 2024, FREYR Battery announced the acquisition of Trina Solar's US solar module manufacturing operations, centred on a 5 GW assembly facility in Wilmer, Texas. The transaction consideration fell in the range of approximately $100 million to $200 million plus the assumption of certain liabilities, with precise terms set out in a Form 8-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The strategic logic was direct. Trina Solar, the Chinese panel manufacturer, had constructed the Wilmer facility to serve the US market and benefit from the IRA's domestic content incentive framework. As the geopolitical and trade landscape shifted — with expanding tariff and supply chain scrutiny applied to Chinese-linked solar manufacturers operating in the United States — the asset became strategically available. For Barcelo's FREYR, Wilmer offered a ready-made, operational solar module manufacturing platform: an existing workforce, established equipment, and customer relationships that could be reoriented under American ownership without the multi-year greenfield construction risk that had weighed so heavily on the battery thesis.

The IRA Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credit anchored the investment case. At $0.07 per watt for completed solar modules, a 5 GW annual manufacturing run rate at Wilmer would generate approximately $350 million per year in Section 45X credits — a figure that dwarfs the acquisition consideration and represents a fundamentally different economic profile than the capital-intensive, pre-revenue battery build-out FREYR had been navigating. Additional incremental credits are available for domestically produced cells and wafers under the same statute.

| Metric | FREYR Battery (battery thesis, pre-pivot) | T1 Energy (solar, Wilmer at scale) |
|---|---|---|
| Primary asset | Mo i Rana CQP, Norway | 5 GW Wilmer, Texas |
| Revenue profile | Pre-commercial | Post-acquisition operational |
| Principal policy support | EU battery sovereignty frameworks | IRA Section 45X ($0.07/W module PTC) |
| Implied 45X credit at nameplate | — | ~$350M / year |
| Principal competitor benchmark | Northvolt, Samsung SDI, CATL | First Solar (FSLR) |

## T1 Energy: The Rename and the Reorientation

In the first quarter of 2025, the company completed its corporate transformation by renaming itself T1 Energy Inc. and relocating its principal headquarters from Luxembourg — the legal domicile inherited from the FREYR Battery SPAC structure — to Austin, Texas. The NYSE ticker changed from FREY to TE. The Luxembourg holding architecture was effectively retired; T1 Energy positioned itself explicitly as a US solar manufacturing company with a secondary retained interest in Norwegian battery development assets.

The Mo i Rana CQP was not divested. Battery cell development continued at reduced priority and reduced funding intensity, with management framing the Norwegian operations as optionality — a potential future platform if capital markets conditions and customer offtake economics improved — rather than a near-term capital deployment priority.

## Forward Catalysts

The post-rename operational agenda centres on three near-term tests. The Wilmer Texas production ramp is the most immediate: the facility was operational at acquisition, but scaling throughput against the 5 GW nameplate requires sustained customer commitments, supply chain integration, and manufacturing yield optimisation across module assembly lines inherited from Trina's prior ownership. Section 45X credit realisation is the second: the $0.07/W module credit is non-refundable but transferable under IRA provisions, and T1's ability to monetise credits efficiently — whether through direct tax liability offset or transferability sales to third-party buyers — will materially determine the 2025 and 2026 reported economics. Third, additional customer announcements: the US solar module supply landscape is consolidating around a small number of domestic manufacturers, with First Solar the dominant scaled competitor; T1's ability to secure utility-scale supply agreements with power developers and independent power producers represents the critical commercial execution test for the post-rename equity.

The residual Mo i Rana strategic posture remains the most structurally ambiguous element of the T1 Energy investment thesis. The Norwegian asset is neither wound down nor actively capitalised — its resolution through sale, joint venture, or eventual restart under different market conditions remained an open strategic question as of the snapshot date.

chapters.title: Solar module technology, residual battery IP, and the Section 45X compliance framework
chapters.body:
When T1 Energy inherited the Wilmer, Texas manufacturing complex from Trina Solar in November 2024, it acquired not merely a 5-gigawatt nameplate capacity but a complete manufacturing lineage in tunnel oxide passivated contact technology — TOPCon — one of the highest-efficiency crystalline-silicon cell architectures in commercial production. That inheritance defined the technical starting point of the company's solar pivot and set the parameters for its Section 45X compliance obligations across what management has described as the principal value-creation event in T1's corporate history.

## TOPCon at Wilmer: Technology Specifications and Competitive Positioning

TOPCon cells employ a thin tunnel oxide layer and a phosphorus-doped polysilicon rear contact surface, enabling higher open-circuit voltages and superior passivation compared with the preceding PERC (passivated emitter and rear contact) architecture. Commercial TOPCon modules from leading producers typically deliver nameplate efficiencies in the 22–24 percent range, compared with approximately 20–22 percent for mainstream mono-PERC product. For a utility-scale procurement buyer, that efficiency premium translates directly into fewer modules per installed watt — reducing balance-of-system cost, land consumption, and racking expenditure across large ground-mount projects.

Trina Solar, which established the Wilmer facility as its primary US manufacturing footprint, had invested in TOPCon production lines as part of a global shift toward next-generation cell architectures. When FREYR Battery closed the acquisition in November 2024, the Wilmer complex carried Trina's process recipes, equipment calibrations, and ongoing supply relationships. T1 Energy's stated task was to operate and expand that infrastructure rather than to redesign it — a critical distinction that reduced technical ramp risk relative to greenfield module development.

The competitive landscape adds context to T1's positioning. First Solar, the dominant incumbent US module manufacturer, produces cadmium telluride thin-film modules at its Ohio and Alabama factories — a fundamentally different cell chemistry with distinct performance characteristics: lower temperature coefficients and greater tolerance for partial shading, qualities that have made First Solar modules a preferred procurement target for certain utility developers. First Solar does not directly substitute for crystalline silicon products across all application segments, however, leaving T1 competing principally against other crystalline silicon producers seeking US manufacturing scale under IRA incentives, and against imported modules still circulating through tariff exemption channels. The multi-year efficiency and reliability documentation inherited from Trina therefore carries material commercial value: project finance lenders require bankable performance history for module procurement, and a validated lineage shortens the qualification cycle for new buyers.

## Section 45X: Credit Mechanics and Compliance Architecture

The economics of the Wilmer investment rest substantially on Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act, which provides advanced manufacturing production tax credits on a per-unit basis for domestically manufactured clean energy components. For completed solar modules, the statutory credit rate is $0.07 per watt of nameplate direct current capacity. At Wilmer's 5-gigawatt annual production capacity, full-rate output would generate up to $350 million annually in 45X module credits before any phase-down adjustment.

Crucially, the credit does not require a tax equity partnership structure or project-level monetisation. It attaches to the manufacturer at the point of production and sale, and under transferability provisions introduced in the IRA, T1 Energy can sell those credits to third-party buyers — generating what is effectively a near-cash revenue stream largely independent of the company's own US taxable income position. That transferability mechanism is particularly relevant for a company of T1's capitalisation, which cannot reliably absorb several hundred million dollars of annual credits against its own tax liability in the near term.

Compliance with Section 45X imposes rigorous production documentation requirements. The manufacturer must substantiate unit output volumes, demonstrate that modules were produced at a qualifying US facility, and satisfy Treasury guidance distinguishing genuine domestic production from final assembly of substantially imported subcomponents. The Trina-inherited manufacturing process — which integrates cell production with module lamination and final assembly at Wilmer — was architected to meet a high bar of domestic value-add. Trina Solar had anticipated IRA-era incentives when developing the facility, and that forward planning provided T1 with a compliance infrastructure already calibrated to the relevant regulatory standard. Post-acquisition, T1's internal compliance team assumed responsibility for the full documentation chain: production and yield logs, equipment provenance records, intercompany supply documentation, and audit trails sufficient for IRS examination.

The 45X module credit phases down beginning in 2030, declining ten percent per year and reaching full expiration for most components by 2032. That sunset creates a defined cash-flow window that concentrates the financial argument for Wilmer in the period from 2025 through 2029 and reinforces the near-term operational imperative to maximise throughput while the credit is intact.

## The Mo i Rana Legacy: Battery IP and Strategic Optionality

FREYR Battery's founding thesis was organised around a licensed manufacturing process from 24M Technologies, the MIT-affiliated developer of semi-solid lithium-ion electrode technology. 24M's approach — suspending active electrode materials in a liquid slurry rather than casting dry electrode films — was designed to reduce capital cost per gigawatt-hour relative to conventional lithium-ion cell production architectures. FREYR's Customer Qualification Plant at Mo i Rana, built out through 2022 and 2023, operationalised that licence in a production context, generating proprietary process data across cell formation cycling, electrolyte filling protocols, and quality control yield curves.

With the strategic pivot to US solar manufacturing, the Mo i Rana intellectual property portfolio entered a period of reduced capital intensity. T1 Energy had not divested the Norwegian assets or publicly terminated the 24M licensing relationship as of May 2026, but deployment of capital had shifted materially toward Wilmer. The CQP data — cell performance characterisation under various formation protocols, yield curve analysis across chemistries, and manufacturing cost benchmarks — represents a body of knowledge whose commercial value depends entirely on whether T1 eventually chooses to license, sell, or reactivate that battery manufacturing pathway.

The asymmetry is notable from an investor perspective. The battery IP consumes management bandwidth and some residual carrying cost while contributing no near-term operating revenue. If the economics of semi-solid battery manufacturing re-emerge as a commercial proposition — driven by energy storage procurement mandates, grid-scale battery pricing inflection, or a strategic acquirer seeking an operational process licence — T1 holds a documented technical position that would be materially costly to rebuild from scratch. For now, it sits as a balance-sheet asset of indeterminate present value, held alongside a Wilmer operating business whose near-term economics, anchored to $0.07 per watt in Section 45X credits across 5 gigawatts, are considerably more legible.

chapters.title: Trina integration, Section 45X framework continuity, First Solar competition, Norway battery resolution
chapters.body:
## Wilmer, Texas: Integration and the Execution Gap

The most proximate risk facing T1 Energy is also the most consequential: whether the company can successfully absorb and scale the Wilmer, Texas solar module manufacturing operations it acquired from Trina Solar in November 2024. The transaction transferred a five-gigawatt facility with an inherited operational team — a structure that on paper reduces greenfield execution risk, but that introduces its own complexities. T1 Energy did not build this plant; it acquired a going concern mid-cycle, with embedded procurement relationships, vendor contracts, and workforce dynamics that were originally calibrated to Trina Solar's balance sheet and corporate priorities.

The principal mitigant is precisely that continuity: Wilmer had been operational pre-close, and T1 inherited the manufacturing floor in running condition. The company was not starting from a concrete pour. Yet the history of US clean-energy manufacturing acquisitions is littered with cautionary examples of acquirers who overestimated their capacity to absorb upstream operational complexity while simultaneously managing a corporate rebranding — T1 completed its rename from FREYR Battery in Q1 2025, just months after closing the Trina deal. Integration and rebranding simultaneously is a management bandwidth test. FY2025, the first year with Wilmer's operations consolidated, is the first real data point; FY2026 will be the first full-year operational stress test. Until multi-quarter throughput and yield data is in the public record, the execution risk remains open.

## Section 45X: The Credit That Runs the Math

The economics of US solar module manufacturing in the IRA era are inseparable from Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act. The framework provides a per-watt advanced manufacturing production tax credit — $0.07 per watt for modules, with additional credits available for cells and wafers manufactured domestically. At five gigawatts of annual module capacity, the implied credit value approaches $350 million per year at full utilization. That is not incidental to T1 Energy's business model; it is the business model's structural spine.

The risk is legislative and political. Section 45X, as enacted under the IRA, runs through 2032 — but the history of US energy tax policy is one of extensions, phase-downs, and periodic congressional uncertainty. A future Congress could amend the credit schedule, introduce domestic content recapture provisions, or subject the framework to reconciliation-driven modification. The 2025 federal budget environment, in which IRA provisions became a recurring target in fiscal negotiations, underscored that no statutory sunset guarantee is politically insulated.

The mitigant is structural: Section 45X is not a loan guarantee or a grant — it is a production tax credit that accrues only on actual manufactured output. It is therefore harder to retroactively claw back from operating manufacturers than a forward-looking subsidy. More practically, US solar module manufacturing has accumulated a political constituency that crosses party lines in Sun Belt states. Wilmer, Texas sits in a state whose congressional delegation has demonstrated pragmatic support for domestic manufacturing incentives. That political geography matters when credit frameworks come under pressure. The concern is the tail risk: a 2027 or 2028 amendment that phases the credit down earlier than 2032 would compress the economic window that justified the Trina acquisition price.

## First Solar and the Competitive Field

T1 Energy does not compete in a vacuum. First Solar (FSLR) is the dominant US solar module pure-play — a manufacturer with a decade-plus head start in thin-film cadmium telluride technology, a balance sheet measured in billions, and a multi-gigawatt US capacity expansion already underway. First Solar's competitive advantages are not easily replicated: its proprietary CdTe technology is outside the crystalline silicon supply chain that connects most US module manufacturers to Asian upstream inputs, giving it structural insulation from certain tariff dynamics that affect silicon-based producers.

T1 Energy's Wilmer facility manufactures silicon-based modules — the dominant global technology format, but one that situates the company in a different competitive and supply-chain position from First Solar. The comparative economics are instructive:

| Metric | First Solar (FSLR) | T1 Energy (TE) |
|---|---|---|
| US module technology | CdTe thin-film | Crystalline silicon |
| US manufacturing capacity | Multi-GW, expanding | 5 GW Wilmer (acquired) |
| Section 45X eligibility | Yes | Yes |
| Supply chain upstream exposure | Low (proprietary) | Moderate (silicon supply chain) |
| Balance sheet scale | Multi-billion USD | Smaller-cap acquirer |

The competitive concern is not that First Solar displaces T1 Energy from the US market — demand for domestically manufactured modules under Section 45X incentives is broad enough to sustain multiple producers. The concern is on customer mix and pricing discipline. Utility-scale and commercial solar developers making long-term module procurement commitments will assess counterparty stability. A smaller-balance-sheet acquirer in the early years of an integration faces more customer qualification friction than an established manufacturer. T1 must demonstrate production reliability and financial staying power to win and retain the off-take relationships that make multi-year capacity meaningful.

## Norway: The Asset That Needs a Resolution

The Mo i Rana, Norway battery development assets — the original thesis of FREYR Battery — remain on T1 Energy's books at reduced priority. The Customer Qualification Plant that consumed significant capital in 2022 and 2023 is not generating material revenue, and the broader US Atlanta gigafactory plans that FREYR Battery once advanced were scaled back during the 2023-2024 strategic reset. What remains is a Norwegian asset with uncertain strategic trajectory in a company whose capital allocation has decisively pivoted to Texas.

The risk is capital drag and management distraction. Every dollar and every executive hour directed at Norway is a dollar and hour not directed at Wilmer scaling. The mitigant — if the Norway asset can be monetized, partnered, or resolved — is that resolution would clean the balance sheet and sharpen the investment narrative. The concern is that the Norwegian battery asset, in a market that has grown deeply skeptical of greenfield lithium-ion gigafactory capital intensity, may be difficult to divest at a value that avoids a material write-down. FREYR Battery's strategic history — from ambitious Norwegian founder Tom Einar Jensen's original vision through the successive scale-backs — has already demonstrated the challenge of realizing gigafactory economics in non-Asian markets. The resolution question is open as of the May 2026 snapshot window.

## US Trade Policy and the Chinese Tariff Architecture

Silicon-based US solar module manufacturing sits at the intersection of IRA industrial policy and a volatile trade environment with Chinese producers. The US solar module market has operated under successive tariff regimes directed at Chinese and Southeast Asian solar product imports — Section 201 safeguard tariffs, Section 301 tariffs, and the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act's supply chain tracing requirements have all shaped the competitive landscape. These measures collectively create a tariff umbrella that elevates the price floor for imported modules, to the benefit of US domestic manufacturers including T1.

The risk is reversal or renegotiation. A US-China trade détente that softened the tariff architecture would compress the price premium available to domestic manufacturers. Separately, the UFLPA supply chain tracing requirements have created operational friction for importers — but a future enforcement softening could reduce the compliance burden that currently disadvantages imports. T1 benefits from the current regime; it has limited ability to influence its continuation.

## Capital Structure: The Adequacy Question

T1 Energy funded the Trina acquisition — consideration in the range of $100 to $200 million plus liability assumption — from a company whose FREYR Battery predecessor had spent the preceding two years managing a capital-intensive battery development program against a backdrop of rising rates and a skeptical public market for pre-revenue energy transition manufacturers. The post-acquisition balance sheet carries the obligations of that history plus the new integration commitments.

The central question is whether T1 has sufficient liquidity runway to reach the phase of Wilmer operations where Section 45X credits are flowing at scale. A slower-than-planned ramp, a customer contract delay, or an unexpected capital expenditure at the facility could create a financing need in a market that has already demonstrated its willingness to punish SPAC-heritage energy transition companies on dilutive equity raises. The mitigant is that Wilmer is not greenfield — the facility's operational base should generate cash earlier than a construction-stage project. But until the P&L from consolidated Wilmer operations is visible across multiple quarters, the adequacy of the capital structure remains an open analytical question that sophisticated investors will weight heavily.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## Execution, not story: the twelve months that will define T1 Energy

The rename is done. The acquisition is booked. The first full year of Wilmer Texas solar module operations is underway. For T1 Energy, the period from mid-2026 through mid-2027 is the interval in which a strategic-pivot narrative either proves itself in shipment volumes, Section 45X credit realisation, and operating leverage — or begins to unravel against the relentless cost competition of imported Asian modules and the political uncertainty surrounding the IRA's advanced manufacturing provisions.

By the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026, T1 Energy has completed approximately two full quarters of consolidated Wilmer Texas operations under its own balance sheet, having closed the Trina Solar acquisition in November 2024 and rebranded in Q1 2025. FY2025 was the company's first year of meaningful module shipment revenue; FY2026 will be the first complete fiscal year in which management can be held to a full-year capacity utilisation target without the one-time accounting noise of purchase-price allocation and organisational integration. That shift — from transition-year to run-rate — is what makes the next twelve months the most consequential since the SPAC listing.

---

## Quarter-by-quarter catalyst map: June 2026 through May 2027

**Q2 2026 results (expected August 2026).** The first unambiguous read on run-rate Wilmer Texas output. By Q2 2026, the post-acquisition integration period should be complete; the operational team inherited from Trina Solar's US business will have had more than eighteen months under T1 ownership. The key numbers: module gigawatts shipped in the quarter, average selling price per watt, and — critically — Section 45X credit dollars booked or receivable. Investors will be watching for consistent, quarter-on-quarter Section 45X credit recognition in the filings. Any shortfall in utilisation here will raise immediate questions about whether demand for the facility's output is keeping pace with supply capacity.

**Wilmer Texas capacity ramp milestone (target: 2026 H2).** Management has indicated ambitions to scale Wilmer Texas toward its nameplate 5 GW annual capacity; any formal announcement of an expanded utilisation corridor or additional module qualification with a US utility or EPC customer would constitute a discrete positive catalyst. The solar module supply chain — wafers, cells, encapsulant, backsheet, glass — has its own lead times, and a 5 GW-nameplate facility running at partial utilisation is a capital-intensity drag. An announcement of multi-year offtake, specifically from a vertically integrated utility-scale developer, would be the clearest positive signal available in this window.

**Q3 2026 results (expected November 2026).** The seasonality test: US solar EPC activity tends to concentrate in Q2–Q3 as developers race to complete installations before winter. Q3 module shipments will reveal whether T1 Energy is capturing peak-season demand or ceding it to more established suppliers. Any IRA policy developments between now and November 2026 — revised Treasury guidance on Section 45X qualification, Congressional action on IRA provisions, or tariff adjustments affecting imported cell costs — will also be live variables. The module manufacturing credit has been a persistent target of policy critics; even a credible legislative threat to the $0.07/W rate would alter the investment case materially.

**Norway battery asset decision (timing uncertain; watch H2 2026).** The Mo i Rana Customer Qualification Plant represents the residual of FREYR Battery's original thesis. Management has maintained Norway battery development at reduced priority since the strategic reset. A formal divestiture, partnership announcement, or structured write-down would clear a narrative overhang that has followed the stock since 2023. The CQP carried capitalised costs from its construction phase; any impairment test outcome in a 2026 annual report will be a clean signal of management's true posture toward the legacy assets — and a test of whether Barcelo is willing to be definitive about closing the battery chapter.

**Q4 2026 and FY2026 results (expected February–March 2027).** The first full-year financial statement with Wilmer Texas at full consolidation. Street consensus models will be calibrated against FY2026 revenue, gross margin, and Section 45X credit realisation as reported. This filing will also contain management's first formal FY2027 guidance — the clearest public statement of how aggressively the executive team expects to scale utilisation into the back half of the decade.

**Q1 2027 results (expected May 2027).** The one-year anniversary of the post-rename operational baseline. Q1 is seasonally softer for solar module shipments, so a strong Q1 2027 would indicate sustainable demand rather than peak-season loading — and would meaningfully reinforce confidence in the full-year FY2027 outlook.

---

## Estimates and the Section 45X arithmetic

Formal sell-side consensus estimates for T1 Energy at this stage of its operating history carry wide dispersion; coverage remains limited relative to the company's market capitalisation, and the ramp-story framing makes bottom-up modelling sensitive to a small number of assumptions. The principal economics driver is not manufacturing margin in the conventional sense but the Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credit under the Inflation Reduction Act — making the credit realisation rate the single most load-bearing number in any financial model.

The IRA's Section 45X framework provides $0.07 per watt for domestically manufactured solar modules, with additional credits available for cells ($0.04/W) and wafers ($0.12/W) where those are also manufactured in the United States. For T1 Energy, which operates the Wilmer Texas module assembly facility but does not, as of the frozen snapshot, manufacture cells or wafers domestically at scale, the base $0.07/W module credit is the relevant figure.

| Scenario | Wilmer Texas utilisation | GW shipped (annual) | 45X credit rate | Implied annual credit value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bear | 20% of 5 GW nameplate | 1.0 GW | $0.07/W | ~$70M |
| Base | 40% of 5 GW nameplate | 2.0 GW | $0.07/W | ~$140M |
| Bull | 70% of 5 GW nameplate | 3.5 GW | $0.07/W | ~$245M |

These Section 45X credit flows are, in the near term, the dominant swing variable in T1 Energy's financials — more important to P&L outcomes than module ASP movement in a range of ±$0.02/W. At the bear-case 20% utilisation, the credit alone barely covers corporate overhead at a company of T1 Energy's scale; at the bull-case 70%, it becomes a substantial and repeatable cash flow contributor that supports a very different equity valuation discussion.

Module ASP pressure from Chinese manufacturers — who remain competitive even in the post-tariff environment, particularly at the cell and wafer level — means that manufacturing margin on modules absent the credit is thin to negative for most US assemblers. The IRA Section 45X credit is not merely supportive; it is structurally load-bearing for the US solar module manufacturing economics at T1's cost position.

---

## Metrics that confirm or break the thesis

**Section 45X credit realisation.** Specifically: dollars of Section 45X credits recognised or receivable per quarter, and the effective per-watt rate achieved. Any shortfall against the $0.07/W base rate would warrant investigation — it could signal qualification issues, shipment timing, or a change in Treasury interpretation. The credit should be a predictable, formulaic line item; volatility in the realised rate is a red flag.

**Wilmer Texas utilisation rate.** GW shipped divided by nameplate capacity, annualised. A sustained utilisation rate below 30% through FY2026 would suggest demand-side constraints that a more favourable macro environment or tariff regime alone cannot solve; above 60% would indicate the facility is genuinely supply-constrained and capacity expansion becomes the next conversation.

**Customer concentration.** Any single customer above 30–35% of quarterly module shipments is a thesis risk. Utility-scale solar development is lumpy; losing one anchor account would show immediately in shipment volumes.

**Norway CQP carrying value and impairment.** The residual book value of the Mo i Rana assets on the balance sheet. An impairment charge — while negative in one-time earnings terms — would clarify management's capital allocation intent and potentially free management bandwidth for the US-facing business.

**Gross margin ex-Section 45X.** Stripping out the credit, what does the underlying module manufacturing margin look like? If ex-credit gross margin is deeply negative, T1 Energy's economics are entirely credit-dependent — a structurally fragile position in any regime where IRA provisions remain politically contested.

---

## What constitutes a beat, and what a miss

A **beat** in the next four quarters would combine: Wilmer Texas utilisation materially above the base-case 40% corridor; Section 45X credit realisation at or close to $0.07/W implying smooth Treasury qualification; a multi-year module offtake agreement with a creditworthy counterpart announced and disclosed in full; and a definitive announcement on the Norway CQP assets — sale, partnership, or structured wind-down — that removes the narrative overhang. Any one of these individually moves the stock; all four in the same quarter would represent a material re-rating event. The definition of a beat is, at this stage, less about absolute earnings per share and more about demonstrating that the Wilmer Texas ramp is tracking toward a 50%-plus utilisation rate by end-FY2026.

A **miss** would be: utilisation stalling below 25% without a clear demand-side explanation; any indication that Treasury is narrowing Section 45X qualification criteria in ways that constrain T1's credit eligibility; significant module ASP compression that turns gross margin deeply negative ex-credit; or — the tail risk — a Congressional action reducing or sunsetting the Section 45X PTC rate on a timeline that materially compresses the investment payback on Wilmer Texas.

---

## The asymmetry: bull and bear setups into May 2027

The bull case rests on three compounding advantages. First, Section 45X credits provide a floor to economics that no Chinese module manufacturer can replicate inside the United States — the credit is, by design, restricted to US-manufactured output, and that asymmetry does not erode with further ASP compression from abroad. Second, Wilmer Texas was an inherited operating asset, not a greenfield build; T1 Energy absorbed a running production line and an experienced operational team, which compresses the commissioning risk that destroyed capital for so many battery and clean-energy start-ups in the 2021–2023 vintage. Third, the tariff environment following 2025–2026 trade policy actions has substantially increased the effective landed cost of imported Chinese modules, widening the pricing window within which US-based assemblers can compete on delivered economics.

The bear case is a tighter argument but no less credible. Section 45X political durability is the central structural risk — manufacturing credits passed in a partisan vote remain vulnerable to a change in Congressional composition, and the debate over IRA provisions has not resolved. Module ASP erosion, driven by persistent global oversupply at the cell and wafer level, compresses the economics even with the credit in place; a US module assembler that does not also manufacture cells domestically operates with inherently thinner margins than a fully vertically integrated peer such as First Solar. And the FREYR Battery heritage is a structural trust deficit: this management team guided investors through a battery-cycle collapse and a full strategic about-face; the capital markets will demand demonstrated execution over an extended period before assigning a premium multiple.

Daniel Barcelo's task for the next twelve months is, in its simplest form, to make the Section 45X arithmetic visible and repeatable in the quarterly filings. The narrative work is complete. The Trina acquisition has been absorbed. The rename has been filed. What remains is the cadence of gigawatts shipped, credits realised, and margin demonstrated — quarter by quarter, with no further strategic pivots available as a fallback if execution disappoints.

chapters.title: Wilmer Texas scaling, Section 45X capture, and the 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Arithmetic of Wilmer

By the time T1 Energy published its first full-year results under the new banner, the strategic logic of the Wilmer Texas acquisition had compressed into a single line of arithmetic. A 5-gigawatt solar module factory operating at capacity against a Section 45X advanced manufacturing production tax credit of $0.07 per watt generates roughly $350 million annually in direct federal credits — before a single dollar of module revenue. For a company that had spent most of its public life explaining to sceptical investors why Norwegian lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing would eventually earn returns, the simplicity was almost disarming.

The Wilmer facility, a roughly 500,000-square-foot plant in the Dallas-Fort Worth exurbs that Trina Solar had built as part of its own US manufacturing push, came with an operational workforce and an already-running production line when FREYR Battery completed the acquisition in November 2024. Unlike the Mo i Rana Customer Qualification Plant, which had absorbed years of capital expenditure before producing a commercially meaningful cell, Wilmer was manufacturing modules before the ink dried on the purchase agreement. That operational inheritance was the core of the acquisition's appeal — and, from Daniel Barcelo's perspective, the answer to the strategic trap his predecessor had walked into.

## Section 45X: Mechanics and Limits

The Inflation Reduction Act's Section 45X framework, enacted in August 2022, established a schedule of per-unit production tax credits for domestically manufactured clean energy components. For solar modules, the credit runs at $0.07 per watt of nameplate capacity through 2029, stepping down thereafter: 75 percent of the prevailing rate in 2030, 50 percent in 2031, 25 percent in 2032, and zero beyond that. Credits attach to production, not to sales, meaning T1 Energy accrues the PTC value at the point of manufacture rather than upon module delivery — a structural advantage that insulates the economics from short-term module pricing pressure and contract timing.

At full 5 GW annual throughput, the implied credit is approximately $350 million per year through the 2029 phase-down trigger. That figure carries important caveats. It assumes the facility is running at nameplate, that the modules meet the statutory definition under Section 45X (domestically manufactured, meeting applicable content requirements), and that the regulatory framework remains intact. As of the snapshot date in May 2026, none of those assumptions was entirely settled. The facility had been ramping, not running flat-out; the broader US solar supply chain for cells and wafers — which carry their own separate Section 45X credits — remained incomplete; and the political durability of the IRA's clean energy provisions had entered a new phase of Congressional contestation.

| Facility capacity | Credit rate (2025-2029) | Implied annual PTC at full output |
|---|---|---|
| 5 GW (nameplate) | $0.07/W | ~$350M/year |
| 3 GW (partial ramp) | $0.07/W | ~$210M/year |
| 1.5 GW (early ramp) | $0.07/W | ~$105M/year |

The step-down schedule gives T1 Energy a compressed window. Full-capacity production in 2026 and 2027 captures the maximum per-watt credit at scale. Each year of delayed ramp-up is not merely a missed revenue quarter — it is a permanent reduction in the credit-weighted value of the investment thesis.

## Ramp Trajectory and Execution Risk

FY2025 was, by design, a consolidation year. T1 inherited Wilmer's operational team and ran the facility through integration, updated offtake relationships, and the corporate restructuring attendant on the Q1 2025 rename and US headquarters relocation to Austin. FY2026 marked the first year in which Barcelo's management had full-year ownership of the production schedule and the full-year Section 45X credit accrual. Investors watching the quarterly cadence were tracking utilisation rates against the nameplate 5 GW ceiling, and the pace of that ascent defined the near-term investment case.

The manufacturing challenge at Wilmer is less technological than logistical. Solar module assembly — tabbing, stringing, lamination, framing — is capital-light relative to cell and wafer production. The constraint is upstream. Trina's original Wilmer operation sourced cells from its own Chinese manufacturing network; under US trade law and the Section 45X framework's domestic content architecture, T1 Energy faced structural pressure to source cells from domestic or non-Chinese suppliers. The emerging US cell manufacturing ecosystem — anchored by facilities from Qcells, Heliene, and others — was itself still ramping in early 2026, creating intermittent supply tightness that constrained Wilmer's throughput independent of T1's own operational choices.

Barcelo has characterised the cell supply question as a medium-term constraint rather than a structural ceiling, pointing to the pipeline of announced US cell capacity as an eventual relief valve. Whether that relief arrives on a schedule aligned with the pre-phase-down credit window remains the central operational uncertainty.

## Competitive Positioning Against First Solar

The US solar module market is not a blank canvas. First Solar, the Tempe-based manufacturer that has operated US production since the 1990s, had approximately 8 GW of US nameplate capacity in its manufacturing network as of early 2026, with further expansion underway in Alabama and Louisiana. First Solar's cadmium telluride thin-film technology is distinct from the crystalline silicon modules that Wilmer produces, which has historically allowed the two companies to serve partly differentiated market segments — First Solar skewing toward utility-scale projects with procurement teams sophisticated enough to specify thin-film, T1's crystalline silicon product more directly interchangeable with the broader global commodity pool.

The competitive pressure T1 Energy faces is not primarily from First Solar but from the broader flood of Southeast Asian module supply rerouted through third countries to avoid US tariffs, and from the possibility that domestic US module pricing converges downward as additional US capacity comes online. The Section 45X credit creates a cost-of-production floor that insulates T1 from import competition in ways that pure market pricing would not, but it does not guarantee offtake pricing. A utility that can buy a US-made module from T1 at $0.28 per watt, knowing T1 is capturing $0.07/W in PTCs, will negotiate hard on the module price — and as more domestic capacity enters the market, the bargaining dynamic shifts.

## Norway: The Residual Question

The Mo i Rana Customer Qualification Plant, the physical embodiment of Tom Einar Jensen's original thesis, remained on T1 Energy's balance sheet as of the snapshot date. Barcelo's public statements positioned the Norwegian battery assets as a retained optionality rather than an active capital commitment — a hedge against a scenario in which the US solar thesis underdelivers and the European battery market recovers sufficiently to justify resumed investment. The practical reality is more constrained. Battery cell manufacturing economics had not materially improved since the 2023-2024 industry reset that accelerated FREYR's strategic pivot, and T1's capital budget was oriented toward Wilmer, not Mo i Rana.

The Norwegian asset presents a balance-sheet overhang that analysts have periodically flagged as a distraction. A sale, a joint-venture arrangement with a European industrial partner, or an outright write-down remained the plausible resolution paths. Each carries its own signalling consequence: a sale crystallises the strategic break cleanly; a write-down acknowledges the impairment without a transaction; a joint venture preserves optionality while reducing the capital drag. None had been executed by May 2026.

## Risks Revisited

The Section 45X durability question has moved from theoretical to proximate. As the 2026 US legislative session progressed, the Inflation Reduction Act's clean energy provisions faced renewed pressure from a Congress that had shifted in composition. The solar module credit was not the most politically vulnerable element of the IRA — the electric vehicle tax credit had drawn more concentrated industry opposition — but the broader architecture of the advanced manufacturing PTC framework was subject to the same fiscal consolidation pressures that were restructuring large portions of the federal budget.

An outright repeal of Section 45X credits would be catastrophic for T1's investment thesis. A phase-down acceleration — compressing the step-down schedule so that the 2029 phase-down arrived in 2027 or 2028 — would be materially damaging without being fatal, provided Wilmer could reach high utilisation before the compression hit. A prospective-only change that preserved credits for modules produced under existing manufacturing commitments would be manageable. As of the snapshot date, the legislative trajectory remained uncertain enough that no outcome could be assigned high confidence.

The secondary risk is module price deflation outpacing the PTC cushion. Global crystalline silicon module prices had been structurally compressed by Chinese manufacturing scale, and the tariff architecture that had kept US module prices above global spot was itself subject to trade policy revision. If the effective US module price declined below the level at which Section 45X credits provided adequate margin, T1's production economics would deteriorate even with the credits intact.

## The Durability of the Thesis

T1 Energy entered the 2026-2030 window as a company whose investment thesis rested on two pillars of uncertain but calculable duration: the operational ramp of Wilmer Texas to a utilisation level that made the Section 45X credit scale meaningful, and the political durability of the IRA framework long enough for that credit to compound into balance-sheet strength. The first pillar was an execution problem — tractable, measurable quarter by quarter, and at least partly within management's control. The second was a legislative problem, beyond management's control and subject to the compressed political cycles that make multi-year industrial policy commitments structurally fragile in the United States.

What distinguished T1 Energy from the battery capital-intensity trap that had consumed its prior strategic identity was the difference between a manufacturing thesis that required years of construction before generating a dollar of credit, and one that had inherited an operating facility on day one. Whether that advantage was durable enough to carry the company through the phase-down window — and whether Barcelo could execute the utilisation ramp before the credit arithmetic shifted against the investment — remained, as of the snapshot date, genuinely open questions.

## Appendix D — IRA Section 45X Advanced Manufacturing PTC Framework

Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act provides per-unit production tax credits for domestically manufactured clean energy components. For solar modules, the credit is **$0.07 per Watt** of capacity. Additional credits attach to solar cells ($0.04/W) and wafers. Credits are claimed against production output, not capital expenditure, making them structurally supportive of operating economics rather than solely capital formation. The framework underpinned T1 Energy's rationale for the November 2024 Trina acquisition and is the central economics lever for Wilmer Texas operations.
